title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Lisbon is one of Europe’s most affordable capitals, and two days here on a tight budget is entirely doable if you prioritise walking, public transport and local eateries. Start your first morning in Alfama, the oldest quarter, where narrow lanes climb toward the castle. Skip the paid castle interior and instead wander the free viewpoints, or miradouros, such as Miradouro de Santa Luzia, which offers sweeping views over the red rooftops to the river. A tram ride on the famous 28 is a budget sightseeing tour in itself, but board early at Martim Moniz to avoid crowds and pickpockets. A single ticket loaded onto a Viva Viagem card keeps costs low; validate as you go.

For lunch, avoid the tourist menus near the main squares and look for a tasca, a small local restaurant. A prato do dia, or plate of the day, with soup, bread and a drink often costs under ten euros. Try bifana, a simple pork sandwich, or a pastel de nata from a neighbourhood bakery for around one euro. In the afternoon, head downhill to Baixa and the riverfront Praça do Comércio, then walk along the water toward Belém if you have the energy, or take a cheap bus. In Belém, the Jerónimos Monastery cloisters charge admission, but the church is free, and the riverside gardens and the Monument to the Discoveries are free to admire from outside. The famous Pastéis de Belém bakery is worth the queue for a warm custard tart.

For dinner, explore the Bairro Alto or Cais do Sodré areas, where inexpensive grill houses serve fresh fish and petiscos, small sharing plates. A glass of vinho verde or a beer costs little. Evening entertainment on a budget means finding a bar with live fado in Alfama, though cover charges vary; some small venues let you listen for the price of a drink. Alternatively, join the locals at a kiosk by a miradouro with a cheap beer and the city lights below.

Day two, start early and take the train from Cais do Sodré to Cascais, a coastal town about forty minutes away, included on a cheap day pass. The journey hugs the river and ocean, and Cascais offers free beaches, a pleasant marina and a market. Pack a picnic from a Lisbon supermarket to keep lunch costs down. Return in the afternoon and use your remaining time to explore the trendy LX Factory, a former industrial complex turned into shops and cafes, free to wander. Or visit the free National Tile Museum on Sundays, when entry is complimentary.

For your final evening, eat at a churrasqueira, a grill restaurant, where half a chicken with rice and salad is a bargain. Finish with a stroll through Praça do Comércio at night, when the arcades are lit and the river breeze is cool. Budget tips: buy a rechargeable Viva Viagem card for metro, tram and bus; drink tap water, which is safe; and remember that many museums are free on Sunday mornings. With cheap eats, walkable neighbourhoods and low-cost transport, two days in Lisbon need not break the bank.

title: grant proposal|a community oral-history project for a public library
text:
Project Title: Voices of the Neighborhood: A Community Oral History Initiative at the Public Library

Applicant Organization: [Name of Public Library]
Funding Requested: [Amount]
Project Duration: Twelve months

Overview

The [Name of Public Library] requests funding to establish Voices of the Neighborhood, a community oral history project designed to document, preserve, and share the lived experiences of local residents. Public libraries serve as trusted civic anchors, and this initiative will position the library as an active steward of community memory. By recording and archiving first-person narratives, the project will create a permanent, freely accessible collection that reflects the diversity of our town and strengthens intergenerational connections.

Statement of Need

Our community has undergone significant demographic and economic change over the past several decades. Longtime residents possess invaluable knowledge about local history, cultural traditions, and neighborhood life, yet much of this knowledge exists only in personal memory and is at risk of being lost. At the same time, newer residents often lack opportunities to learn about the place they now call home. There is currently no systematic effort in our area to capture these stories. The library is uniquely positioned to fill this gap: it is trusted, free to all, and committed to equitable access to information. This project directly advances the library's mission to serve as a center for lifelong learning and community engagement.

Project Goals and Objectives

Goal 1: Collect and preserve at least forty recorded oral history interviews from a diverse cross-section of residents, including elders, immigrants, longtime business owners, and community leaders.
Goal 2: Build a searchable digital archive, hosted on the library's website, with transcripts and audio files accessible to the public.
Goal 3: Foster community dialogue through public programming, including an oral history training workshop, a series of listening sessions, and a culminating community celebration.

Activities and Timeline

Months 1 to 3: Hire and train a part-time project coordinator, purchase recording equipment, and recruit volunteers through local partnerships with senior centers, schools, and cultural organizations.
Months 4 to 9: Conduct interviews, complete transcriptions, and begin uploading content to the digital archive. Host two volunteer training workshops on interviewing techniques and ethical documentation.
Months 10 to 12: Launch the public archive, host a community listening event, and publish a printed companion booklet featuring selected excerpts.

Evaluation

Success will be measured through the number of interviews completed and archived, volunteer participation rates, archive usage statistics, and participant satisfaction surveys. A final report will be submitted to the funder and shared with the library board and community partners.

Budget Summary

The requested funds will support the part-time project coordinator, recording and transcription equipment, transcription services, volunteer training materials, and modest costs for the community celebration. The library will contribute in-kind support, including staff time, meeting space, and marketing assistance.

Conclusion

Voices of the Neighborhood will transform our library from a repository of books into a living archive of community memory. By capturing the stories that define our town, this project will ensure that future generations can hear, learn from, and be inspired by the voices of those who came before them. We respectfully request the committee's support for this initiative.

title: product review|a mid-range noise-cancelling headphone after three months of use
text:
Three Months With the Sony WH-CH720N: A Working Musician's Honest Take

I bought the Sony WH-CH720N on February 17, 2025, after my trusty Audio-Technica ATH-ANC700BT finally gave up the ghost. Three months and roughly 340 hours of use later—across commutes on the L train, two recording sessions, a flight to Austin, and countless hours at my kitchen table—I have a clear picture of what these $149 headphones do well and where they stumble.

The noise cancelling is the headline, with caveats. Sony's V1 processor, borrowed from the flagship WH-1000XM5, handles low-frequency rumble impressively. The subway's screech drops to a dull hum, and on my Austin flight the engine drone practically vanished. But voices and higher frequencies slip through more than on the XM5s I tested at B&H in March. If you need to silence a chatty open office, these are good, not great.

Sound quality punches above the price. The 30mm drivers deliver a warm, bass-forward signature that suits hip-hop and electronic music, though classical recordings reveal a slightly recessed midrange. I A/B tested them against my Sennheiser HD 560S (wired, open-back, $199) using Fleetwood Mac's "Rumours" on vinyl rips, and the Sony held its own on the low end while losing detail in the upper mids. The companion app's five-band EQ helps—I nudged 400Hz up by two notches and it opened things considerably.

Comfort and battery are where these shine. At 192 grams, they're lighter than the XM5s' 250 grams, and I regularly wore them for four-hour stretches without jaw fatigue. Sony claims 35 hours with ANC on; I measured about 31 hours per charge across three cycles, which is close enough. A 10-minute charge gave me roughly 4.5 hours—genuinely useful when I forgot to plug them in before a morning commute.

The frustrations are real, though. The plastic build creaks when I turn my head sharply, and the earcups don't swivel flat, which makes the included pouch awkward. Multipoint pairing—connecting to my MacBook and iPhone simultaneously—worked flawlessly for two months, then started dropping the laptop connection after the April 3 firmware update (version 2.1.0). Sony's support suggested a factory reset, which fixed it for about a week before it recurred. The touch controls also misfire in cold weather; I've accidentally skipped tracks with a scarf brushing the right earcup more times than I can count.

Verdict: At $149—I've seen them dip to $119 during Amazon's spring sale—the WH-CH720N is a sensible buy for commuters and casual listeners who want competent ANC without flagship pricing. But if multipoint reliability matters for your workflow, or you need to silence human voices specifically, stretch to the $279 XM4s or look at the $199 Bose QuietComfort SE. These are good headphones with a few honest compromises—which, at this price, feels like a fair trade.

title: market research report|consumer demand for electric bicycles in Europe
text:
Consumer Demand for Electric Bicycles in Europe

Market Research Report — Section 4: Demand Dynamics and Consumer Behaviour

 Overview

Electric bicycles have moved decisively from niche product to mainstream consumer good across Europe. Following a period of exceptional growth between 2019 and 2022, demand has settled into a more measured but structurally robust pattern. Industry data indicate that e-bikes now account for a substantial and rising share of total bicycle sales by value in most Western European markets, with the segment proving markedly more resilient than the conventional bicycle market during the recent period of inventory correction. The central question for stakeholders is no longer whether demand exists, but how it is segmenting, maturing and varying across geographies.

 Principal Demand Drivers

Three factors underpin sustained consumer interest. First, urban mobility policy: congestion charges, low-emission zones and the proliferation of cycle lanes in cities such as Paris, Amsterdam, Berlin and Copenhagen have raised the relative attractiveness of two-wheeled transport. Second, cost economics: for commuters substituting car journeys, e-bikes offer favourable running costs, and employer-supported purchase schemes—notably in Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany—materially reduce the effective purchase price. Third, demographic reach: the electrically assisted format has widened cycling's appeal to older consumers, to those with longer or hillier commutes, and to households previously deterred by physical exertion or distance.

 Segmentation and Consumer Profiles

Demand is increasingly differentiated. The commuter segment remains the largest by volume, concentrated in urban and peri-urban areas and skewed toward higher-income professionals. The leisure and touring segment is growing, particularly in Germany, Austria and France, where long-distance cycle routes and e-MTB categories command premium prices. A third segment—cargo and family logistics—remains smaller in absolute terms but exhibits strong growth in dense cities, supported by subsidy schemes in several municipalities. Replacement demand is also becoming significant: early adopters are now trading up, favouring integrated batteries, mid-drive motors and connected features.

 Geographic Variation

Demand intensity varies considerably by market. Germany remains the largest single market by volume and value, followed by France, the Netherlands and Belgium, where penetration is already high and growth therefore depends on replacement and premiumisation rather than first-time purchase. Southern and Eastern European markets—Italy, Spain, Poland—show faster percentage growth from a lower base, supported by expanding tourism infrastructure and national incentive programmes. Nordic markets display strong uptake in commuting and cargo applications.

 Constraints on Demand

Several factors temper the outlook. Average selling prices remain elevated relative to conventional bicycles, and price sensitivity has increased as household budgets tighten. Battery costs, supply-chain normalisation and the recent wave of discounting have introduced margin pressure across the channel. Regulatory uncertainty—including debates over insurance, licensing and battery safety standards—may affect consumer confidence in some markets. Finally, infrastructure remains uneven: demand is strongest where protected cycling networks are most developed, suggesting that public investment is a binding constraint on further growth.

 Outlook

The trajectory points to continued volume growth at a moderate pace, with value growth outpacing units as premiumisation continues. The most significant upside lies in cargo logistics, replacement cycles and the expansion of employer incentive schemes; the principal risks are price resistance, regulatory friction and infrastructure bottlenecks. Stakeholders should plan for a market that is maturing rather than decelerating—one in which competitive advantage will rest on brand trust, service networks and battery technology rather than on category novelty.

title: BBC-style news article|a football club fined after fans invade the pitch
text:
A football club has been fined heavily after a large number of its supporters invaded the pitch during a match, in an incident that has prompted fresh calls for stricter crowd control measures at stadiums across the country.

The club was ordered to pay a financial penalty reported to be in the region of several hundred thousand pounds following the disturbances, which occurred in the closing minutes of a fiercely contested league fixture. Supporters surged over the advertising hoardings and on to the playing surface after a late goal sparked chaotic scenes, forcing match officials to suspend play for several minutes.

Television pictures showed stewards struggling to contain the crowds as dozens of fans ran across the pitch, some appearing to taunt opposing players and supporters. A number of flares were also set off in the stands, sending plumes of smoke drifting across the stadium. The referee led both teams from the field temporarily before play resumed amid a heavy security presence.

The governing body confirmed the sanction in a statement, saying the club had been found guilty of failing to ensure that its supporters did not encroach on to the field of play. It said the penalty reflected the seriousness of the incident and the potential risk to players, officials and stewards. The club has also been warned about its future conduct and could face further disciplinary action, including the possibility of partial stadium closures, should similar scenes be repeated.

In its written reasons, the disciplinary panel noted that the invasion had been "entirely foreseeable" given the charged atmosphere inside the ground and criticised the club for what it described as inadequate pre-match planning. It added that the safety of those inside the stadium had been compromised and that such behaviour risked bringing the game into disrepute.

The club said it was "deeply disappointed" by the conduct of a minority of supporters and confirmed it would accept the punishment. A spokesperson said the club had already begun a review of its stewarding and ticketing arrangements and would work closely with the police to identify those responsible. "The overwhelming majority of our supporters behaved impeccably, and we apologise to them and to the visiting club for the actions of a small number of individuals," the spokesperson added. The club said it expected to issue banning orders to those found to have taken part.

Players' representatives have renewed their concerns about pitch invasions, arguing that they leave footballers and officials exposed to unnecessary risk. The players' union has repeatedly urged clubs and authorities to treat such incidents with the utmost seriousness, warning that it is only a matter of time before someone is seriously hurt.

Police said they had made a number of arrests and were continuing to examine footage in an effort to identify further offenders. The Football Association is expected to issue updated guidance to clubs before the end of the season, reminding them of their obligations to maintain order and protect those inside the stadium. Campaigners say the latest case underlines the need for a coordinated approach involving clubs, police and supporters' groups to prevent a repeat of the disorder.

title: NGO policy brief|improving childhood nutrition in rural Kenya
text:
POLICY BRIEF
To: Ministry of Health, Division of Nutrition and Dietetics; County Health Executives, Kitui and Kilifi
From: Executive Director, Tumaini Food Security Initiative (TFSI)
Date: 14 March 2025
Subject: Scaling the Malezi Bora Plus model to cut rural child stunting by a third by 2028

The problem in brief

Kenya's 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS) put national stunting at 18 per cent—but the figure masks a rural crisis. In Kitui County our baseline survey of 1,840 children under five, conducted between June and August 2024 across Mwingi Central and Kitui Rural, found stunting at 31.4 per cent. In Kilifi's Ganze sub-county the rate was 29.8 per cent. Only 12 per cent of caregivers in our sample met the minimum acceptable diet standard. The drivers are not mysterious: prolonged drought since the 2021–2023 failure of the long rains, maize prices that peaked at KES 5,800 per 90kg bag in March 2023, and a health workforce gap of one nutritionist per 48,000 people in Kitui.

What we tested

Between January 2023 and December 2024, TFSI ran the Malezi Bora Plus pilot in 24 community health units in Kitui and Kilifi, funded by a KES 210 million grant from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and co-financed by the two county governments. The model had three components: monthly growth monitoring linked to a simplified counselling script delivered by 312 trained community health promoters (CHPs); a fortified porridge voucher redeemable at 46 local agro-dealers; and mother-to-mother support groups meeting fortnightly.

What the evidence shows

An endline evaluation by the African Population and Health Research Center (APHRC), completed in February 2025, found stunting in the pilot sites fell from 31.4 to 24.1 per cent in Kitui and from 29.8 to 23.6 per cent in Kilifi over 24 months—a 7.3 and 6.2 percentage point decline respectively, against a 1.9 point decline in comparison sites. Minimum acceptable diet adherence rose to 41 per cent. Cost per child reached was KES 4,300 annually, roughly a third of the cost of treating severe acute malnutrition in hospital.

Recommendations

1. Adopt Malezi Bora Plus as county policy in Kitui and Kilifi by October 2025, with the CHP counselling script incorporated into the existing Community Health Services training curriculum. TFSI will second its training team at no cost for the first year.

2. Ring-fence KES 180 million in the FY2025/26 county nutrition budgets to sustain the fortified porridge voucher. Treasury should treat this as recurrent expenditure, not donor-dependent programming; the pilot's 2026 expiry date makes transition planning urgent.

3. Close the workforce gap. The Public Service Commission should approve 60 additional nutritionist posts across the two counties, prioritising sub-counties where stunting exceeds 28 per cent.

4. Institutionalise the mother-to-mother groups under the existing Malezi Bora campaign, using the Ministry's April and October health weeks as delivery anchors.

The ask

We request a meeting with the Division of Nutrition and Dietetics before 30 April 2025 to agree a costed transition plan. The full APHRC evaluation is available on request.

*Tumaini Food Security Initiative, Nairobi. Contact: programmes@tumainifsi.org.ke*

title: medical patient information leaflet|managing type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise
text:
Managing Type 2 Diabetes Through Diet and Exercise

Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition in which the body either does not produce enough insulin or does not respond properly to it, causing blood glucose levels to rise. While medication is often necessary, diet and physical activity remain the foundations of effective management. For many people, sustained changes to eating habits and daily movement can significantly improve blood glucose control, reduce cardiovascular risk, and lessen the need for medication over time. This section outlines the principles behind these changes and offers practical guidance.

Dietary approach

There is no single "diabetic diet." The aim is a balanced, sustainable pattern of eating that controls blood glucose, supports a healthy weight, and reduces the risk of complications. The following principles apply broadly:

- Carbohydrate awareness. Carbohydrates have the greatest effect on blood glucose. Choosing wholegrain varieties, pulses, and vegetables over refined carbohydrates and sugary foods produces a slower, smaller rise in glucose. Spreading carbohydrate intake evenly across the day helps avoid peaks and troughs.
- Portion control. Reducing portion sizes, particularly of starchy foods, supports weight management and glucose control. The NHS advises that starchy foods should make up around a third of each meal, alongside plenty of vegetables.
- Fibre. Aim for at least 30g of fibre daily from wholegrains, beans, lentils, fruit, and vegetables. Fibre slows glucose absorption and improves satiety.
- Sugar and processed foods. Limit free sugars—found in sweets, sugary drinks, and many processed products—and keep ultra-processed foods to a minimum. Sugary drinks are best avoided entirely.
- Alcohol. If you drink, keep within national guidelines and be aware that alcohol can cause hypoglycaemia, particularly if you take insulin or sulfonylureas.

Weight loss is particularly important. For people with type 2 diabetes who are overweight, losing 5–10% of body weight can improve HbA1c and may, in some cases, lead to remission when achieved soon after diagnosis. A structured, gradual approach is more likely to be maintained than a restrictive one.

Physical activity

Regular activity increases insulin sensitivity, lowers blood glucose, and supports weight control. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week—such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming—spread across several days, plus two sessions of resistance exercise to maintain muscle mass.

- Start where you are. Any increase in activity is beneficial. Short, frequent bouts of movement, such as a ten-minute walk after meals, can meaningfully lower post-meal glucose.
- Reduce sedentary time. Breaking up long periods of sitting with brief activity is beneficial even if you meet weekly targets.
- Monitor and prepare. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, check your blood glucose before and after new or strenuous activity, and carry fast-acting carbohydrate in case of hypoglycaemia.
- Foot care. Check your feet regularly after exercise, as reduced sensation can allow minor injuries to go unnoticed.

Working with your healthcare team

Diet and exercise changes should be agreed with your GP or diabetes team, particularly if you take medication, as doses may need adjustment. Ask about structured education programmes such as DESMOND, which provide evidence-based support for self-management. Set realistic, specific goals—for example, a daily walk or one dietary change per week—and review them at your regular check-ups. Small, consistent changes sustained over months and years are more effective than short periods of intensive effort.

title: congressional research report|the history and current debate over agricultural subsidies
text:
Agricultural subsidies have been a cornerstone of federal farm policy since the 1930s, when the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 created the first comprehensive system of price supports and production controls in response to the Great Depression and the Dust Bowl. The original goals were to stabilize farm incomes, conserve soil, and ensure a reliable food supply. Over the ensuing decades, Congress repeatedly reauthorized and reshaped these programs through periodic farm bills, shifting from supply management and parity pricing toward direct payments, countercyclical supports, and subsidized crop insurance. The 1996 Freedom to Farm Act attempted to phase out traditional subsidies in favor of fixed, declining payments, but a collapse in commodity prices led Congress to restore ad hoc emergency payments, and subsequent farm bills in 2002, 2008, 2014, and 2018 entrenched a durable framework of income supports, conservation programs, and heavily subsidized insurance. The 2018 farm bill, most recently extended, authorizes roughly $428 billion in spending over five years, with nutrition assistance (SNAP) accounting for about 80 percent and the remainder split among commodity programs, crop insurance, and conservation.

The current debate centers on several interrelated questions. First, distributional equity: critics across the political spectrum argue that subsidy benefits flow disproportionately to large farms and wealthy operators, while small and beginning farmers receive little. Payment limits and eligibility rules have been tightened incrementally, but loopholes persist. Second, market distortion and trade: economists debate whether commodity programs and insurance subsidies encourage overproduction, inflate land values, and disadvantage developing-country producers. World Trade Organization disciplines constrain certain payments, and trading partners have repeatedly challenged U.S. programs, though the WTO dispute system is currently weakened. Third, risk and climate: proponents defend subsidies as essential risk management in a volatile, weather-dependent sector, while critics argue that crop insurance and commodity supports should be conditioned on conservation practices and that funding should shift toward climate-smart agriculture and conservation. Fourth, budget pressure: with the farm bill extension expiring and baseline costs rising, especially for crop insurance and SNAP, lawmakers face difficult tradeoffs. Fifth, equity and nutrition: the longstanding coalition linking farm programs to nutrition assistance has frayed, with some members seeking to separate the two and impose new work requirements on SNAP recipients, complicating reauthorization.

The debate is also shaped by structural change in agriculture. Farm consolidation continues, with fewer, larger operations producing most output, raising questions about whether subsidies sustain family farms or accelerate consolidation by capitalizing into land prices. Meanwhile, specialty crop growers, livestock producers, and organic farmers argue that commodity-focused programs shortchange them. International obligations, disaster aid ad hoc spending, and the rising cost of crop insurance—now the largest farm safety-net expenditure—all feature prominently. Some proposals would cap insurance subsidies for high-income operations, means-test commodity payments, or convert supports into block grants, while others would expand reference prices and strengthen the safety net. Given divided government and competing priorities, the outlook for a new farm bill remains uncertain, and a further extension of current law is plausible. The core tension—between providing a stable safety net for producers and ensuring that public dollars are equitable, fiscally responsible, trade-compliant, and aligned with conservation goals—will define the next chapter of agricultural subsidy policy.

title: court opinion summary|a dispute over a contractor's failure to complete a home renovation
text:
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
NORTHERN DISTRICT OF ILLINOIS
EASTERN DIVISION

MARGARET ELLISON and DAVID ELLISON, Plaintiffs, v. NORTHSHORE RENOVATION & DESIGN, LLC and THOMAS BRENNAN, Defendants.

Case No. 23-cv-04817
Hon. Elaine M. Castellano
Filed: March 14, 2025

OPINION AND ORDER

This matter comes before the Court on cross-motions for summary judgment arising from a failed residential renovation in Evanston, Illinois. For the reasons set forth below, Plaintiffs' motion is granted in part, Defendants' motion is denied, and judgment is entered for Plaintiffs in the amount of $148,650.

I. Background

In February 2022, the Ellisons executed a fixed-price construction contract with Northshore Renovation & Design for a kitchen and first-floor addition to their home on Asbury Avenue. The contract price was $212,000, with a completion date of October 15, 2022. Thomas Brennan, Northshore's sole member, signed on the company's behalf and personally guaranteed the project's timely completion in a side letter dated February 9, 2022.

Work began on March 7, 2022. By August, the project had fallen behind schedule. The parties dispute the cause: Northshore attributes delays to the Village of Evanston's permitting office, while the Ellisons point to Northshore's decision to reassign its crew to a commercial job in Skokie. The record establishes that Northshore abandoned the site entirely on November 18, 2022, after receiving $168,400 in progress payments—roughly 79% of the contract price—while the project was approximately 55% complete according to the report of Plaintiffs' expert, architect Gerald Pappas.

The Ellisons obtained three replacement bids. The lowest, from Whitfield Builders, came in at $193,200 to finish the work. After deducting the unpaid contract balance of $43,600, the Ellisons' net completion cost was $149,600. They filed suit on July 19, 2023, alleging breach of contract, violation of the Illinois Home Repair and Remodeling Act (815 ILCS 513/1 *et seq.*), and breach of the personal guaranty.

II. Analysis

A. Breach of Contract

Defendants argue that the delays were excusable and that the Ellisons' own change orders—seven in total, adding $9,300—reset the schedule. This argument fails. The change orders were minor and signed contemporaneously; none extended the completion date beyond a two-week accommodation the Ellisons granted in September 2022. Under *Osten v. Shah*, 2013 IL App (1st) 112812, a contractor's unilateral walk-off is a material breach excusing further performance by the owner. Northshore's abandonment on November 18, 2022, is undisputed. Plaintiffs are entitled to the reasonable cost of completion, measured by the Whitfield bid.

B. Home Repair and Remodeling Act

Northshore violated Section 30 of the Act by failing to provide the Ellisons with the required "Home Repair: Know Your Consumer Rights" pamphlet before signing. Defendants concede noncompliance but argue the Act affords no private right of action. This Court has previously held otherwise, and the Illinois Supreme Court's reasoning in *Kunkel v. Walton*, 179 Ill. 2d 519 (1997), supports the availability of actual damages for a violation that permeates the formation of the contract. However, because Plaintiffs' damages under the Act are coextensive with their contract damages, no separate recovery is awarded.

C. Personal Guaranty

Brennan's February 9, 2022 letter states: "I personally guarantee that Northshore will complete the Ellison project by October 15, 2022, or I will pay for any reasonable costs of completion." That language is unambiguous. Brennan's argument that the guaranty required a separate signature is unavailing; the letter bears his signature and identifies the consideration. He is jointly and severally liable.

III. Damages

Plaintiffs seek $149,600 in completion costs, $6,400 for a failed rough-in inspection that Whitfield was required to correct, and $3,750 in architectural fees for Pappas's remediation plan. Defendants do not contest the reasonableness of the Pappas fee. The Court reduces the completion figure by $1,100, reflecting a credit for appliances Northshore purchased and left on site. Total damages: $148,650.

IV. Conclusion

Defendants' motion for summary judgment is denied. Plaintiffs' motion is granted. Judgment is entered for Margaret and David Ellison and against Northshore Renovation & Design, LLC and Thomas Brennan, jointly and severally, in the amount of $148,650, plus prejudgment interest at 5% from November 18, 2022, and costs.

SO ORDERED.

Elaine M. Castellano
United States District Judge

title: technical documentation|configuring a home network router for parental controls
text:
Configuring Parental Controls on a Home Router

Parental controls allow administrators to restrict access to inappropriate content, limit screen time, and monitor network activity for designated devices. Most consumer routers manufactured within the past five years include some form of content filtering, though the depth of these features varies considerably by vendor. This section explains how to locate, configure, and maintain parental control settings on a typical home router. Administrators should note that router-level controls apply to all traffic on the network and cannot be bypassed by clearing browser history or using a device's private browsing mode, though they can be circumvented by savvy users employing VPNs or cellular data.

 Prerequisites

Before configuring parental controls, confirm the following:

- Administrative access to the router's web interface. Credentials are typically printed on a label affixed to the device, or were established during initial setup.
- A stable connection to the router, either via Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
- The MAC addresses of devices to be restricted. These are usually found in the device's network settings or in the router's list of connected clients.

 Accessing the Router Interface

Open a web browser and enter the router's default gateway address—commonly 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1—into the address bar. Consult the router's documentation if neither address responds. Enter the administrator username and password when prompted. If the default credentials have never been changed, do so now; routers shipped with factory-default passwords are a well-documented security risk.

 Locating Parental Control Settings

Menu structures differ across manufacturers. On most routers, parental controls appear under a heading such as "Parental Controls," "Access Restrictions," or "Family Settings." Some vendors separate content filtering from time-based scheduling, requiring configuration in two distinct panels. Administrators should review the router's manual if the relevant options cannot be located within the primary navigation.

 Configuring Content Filters

Content filtering typically operates by one of two methods: category-based blocking, in which the router consults a maintained database of known domains, or manual allow/deny lists. Category-based filtering is generally preferable for households with children, as it requires less ongoing maintenance. Select the categories to block—common options include adult content, gambling, and social media—and assign the policy to the target devices. Where the router supports per-device profiles, create a separate profile for each child rather than applying a single blanket policy.

 Setting Access Schedules

Time-based restrictions allow administrators to define periods during which a device may access the internet. Configure schedules according to household routines: for example, blocking access after 21:00 on school nights while permitting later access on weekends. Note that schedules apply to the device, not the user; a child with access to a second device may circumvent the restriction unless that device is also enrolled.

 Verifying and Maintaining the Configuration

After applying settings, test them from the restricted device by attempting to reach a blocked category or by accessing the network outside the permitted hours. Save the configuration and, if the router supports it, export a backup. Review the settings quarterly: content databases require updates, new devices must be added to profiles, and children's needs change as they mature. Finally, inform household members that filtering is in place. Covert monitoring tends to damage trust, and transparency about the rules—and their rationale—is more effective than silence.

title: wire news story|a central bank holds interest rates steady amid slowing inflation
text:
WASHINGTON, March 18, 2026 (Wire) — The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady on Wednesday, keeping borrowing costs unchanged for a third consecutive meeting as policymakers weighed signs that inflation is cooling against a labor market that remains stubbornly resilient.

The central bank's rate-setting committee voted unanimously to maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 4.25% to 4.50%, a level it has held since January after a series of cuts last year. The decision was widely anticipated by financial markets, with futures pricing before the announcement indicating a better than 90% probability of no change.

In its post-meeting statement, the committee said inflation "has continued to ease" but remains somewhat above its 2% target, while economic activity has expanded at a moderate pace. Policymakers reiterated that they would carefully assess incoming data before adjusting rates further, language that analysts read as a signal the central bank is in no hurry to move.

The pause comes as the latest government data showed consumer prices rising 2.6% in February from a year earlier, down from 3.1% in December and the slowest annual pace since early 2024. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, eased to 2.8%, continuing a gradual descent that has reassured officials the disinflation trend remains intact despite occasional bumps.

"With inflation moving in the right direction and the labor market holding up, the committee has the luxury of patience," said Ellen Marsh, chief economist at Harbor Point Advisors. "Today's decision is less about what the Fed is doing and more about what it is not doing — it is not rushing, and it is not signaling a pivot."

The jobless rate stood at 4.1% last month, and employers added a solid 165,000 jobs, suggesting the economy has not cracked under the weight of elevated rates. Consumer spending has remained positive, though retail sales softened in January, and surveys of business sentiment have been mixed.

Fed Chair Laura Chen, speaking at a news conference after the meeting, said the committee was "encouraged but not complacent" about the inflation outlook. She declined to specify a timeline for further rate cuts, telling reporters that policy would remain "meeting by meeting and data by data." Chen also acknowledged that uncertainty around trade policy and global demand posed risks to the outlook, without elaborating.

Markets reacted modestly to the decision. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note ticked down two basis points, and major stock indexes were little changed in afternoon trading. The dollar held steady against a basket of major currencies.

Attention now turns to the Fed's updated economic projections, which will be released at its next meeting in June. In December, most officials projected two additional quarter-point cuts this year. Wednesday's statement did not address the projections, and Chen said the committee would revisit them as more data arrives.

Some economists cautioned that the recent improvement in inflation could prove fleeting, particularly if energy prices rebound or tariff measures push goods costs higher. Others argued the central bank risks falling behind if the labor market weakens abruptly.

"Staying on hold is the easy call today," said Daniel Okafor, a strategist at Ridgeline Capital. "The harder question is whether the Fed waits too long. Every meeting without a move raises the bar for the next one."

The next policy meeting is scheduled for June 17-18.

Government Audit Report on Oversight of Veterans' Disability Claim Processing Times

Report Number: GA-2025-017
Issuing Office: Office of the Inspector General, Department of Veterans Affairs
Date of Issue: June 12, 2025

Executive Summary

This report presents the findings of an audit conducted to assess the effectiveness of management oversight regarding the processing times of veterans' disability compensation claims. The audit was initiated in response to persistent concerns raised by veterans' service organizations and congressional stakeholders regarding delays in claim adjudication and the consistency of oversight mechanisms within the Veterans Benefits Administration.

The audit examined claims processing data for the period from October 2023 through March 2025, reviewed internal oversight policies and procedures, and conducted interviews with supervisory personnel at four regional benefit offices. The objective was to determine whether existing oversight controls adequately identify, monitor, and address processing delays in a timely and consistent manner.

Background

The Veterans Benefits Administration is responsible for adjudicating disability compensation claims submitted by veterans. Timely processing of these claims is critical to ensuring that veterans receive the benefits to which they are entitled without undue delay. Prior audits and external reviews have repeatedly identified processing delays as a significant risk to program integrity and veteran satisfaction. In response, the agency established performance metrics and oversight controls intended to monitor claim processing times and prompt corrective action when delays occur.

Audit Findings

The audit identified several deficiencies in the oversight of claims processing times. First, performance metrics used to monitor processing times were inconsistently applied across regional offices. Although national targets exist, offices exercised considerable discretion in defining when a claim was considered complete for reporting purposes, resulting in data that did not reliably reflect actual processing times experienced by veterans.

Second, supervisory review of aging claims was not conducted with sufficient frequency. In two of the four offices reviewed, claims exceeding established age thresholds were not systematically flagged for supervisory review, and documentation of corrective actions was incomplete or absent. This weakened the agency's ability to identify bottlenecks and intervene before delays became prolonged.

Third, the audit found that oversight reporting to senior leadership focused primarily on aggregate averages rather than on the distribution of processing times. As a result, persistently delayed individual claims were obscured within favorable overall statistics, limiting management's visibility into areas requiring targeted intervention.

Finally, staffing and workload data were not consistently integrated into oversight reports. This omission hindered the agency's capacity to correlate processing delays with resource shortages and to make informed decisions regarding workload allocation.

Recommendations

The audit makes four recommendations. The agency should standardize the definition of claim completion and enforce consistent application of performance metrics across all regional offices. Supervisory review of aging claims should be conducted at defined intervals, with documented corrective actions subject to periodic quality review. Oversight reporting to senior leadership should include distributional data on processing times, including the number and age of claims exceeding established thresholds. Finally, staffing and workload data should be integrated into routine oversight reports to support resource planning.

Conclusion

While the agency has established a framework for overseeing claims processing times, the audit concludes that this framework is not consistently implemented and does not provide management with a complete picture of processing performance. Implementation of the recommendations in this report will strengthen oversight controls and better ensure that veterans receive timely decisions on their claims.

Management Response

Management concurred with all four recommendations and provided corrective action plans with implementation timeframes ranging from six to twelve months. The Office of the Inspector General will monitor implementation and report periodically on progress.

title: op-ed column|why cities should ban cars from their historic centres
text:
The Case for Pedestrianising the Past

Every summer, the same ritual unfolds in the historic hearts of Europe's cities. Tourists shuffle shoulder to shoulder through medieval squares, guidebooks held aloft, while delivery vans nose through the crowd and taxis idle at the kerb. The air hangs thick with diesel and diesel-fuelled tempers. It is a scene that city leaders have grown oddly resigned to, as though the congestion of a fifteenth-century street were an immutable fact of nature rather than a policy choice. It is not. Cities should ban private cars from their historic centres—and they should do so not as a grudging concession to tourists or environmentalists, but as an act of intelligent stewardship.

The case begins with the fabric of the place itself. Historic centres were built for a world of carts, horses and pedestrians, not for vehicles weighing two tonnes and travelling at speed. Narrow lanes, blind corners and ancient paving stones were never designed to bear the load. In Britain alone, councils have spent hundreds of millions of pounds repairing roads and pavements damaged by traffic that the streets were never engineered to carry. The vibration of passing lorries loosens foundations; the pollution from exhausts corrodes stone and erodes the very facades that draw visitors in the first place. To preserve a historic centre while permitting unfettered car traffic is to saw at the branch on which the local economy sits.

The environmental case is equally straightforward. Urban road transport accounts for a substantial share of nitrogen dioxide and particulate emissions, and concentrations are typically highest in exactly those dense, enclosed streets where dispersion is poorest. Residents of historic centres—often older, often poorer, often living in flats without gardens—bear the brunt. A ban on private cars is among the fastest-acting public health interventions available to a mayor. It costs comparatively little, delivers results within months, and requires no new technology.

But the strongest argument is the one least often made: that cars degrade the civic value of these places. A historic centre is not merely a collection of listed buildings; it is a public inheritance, a stage on which civic life has been performed for centuries. When through-traffic is removed, something remarkable happens. Streets fill with people who linger rather than pass through. Pavement cafes appear. Children walk to school unaccompanied. The noise floor drops, and conversation becomes possible. Studies of pedestrianised zones across Europe consistently find that retail turnover rises, not falls, once car access is restricted—a finding that never fails to surprise the shopkeepers who fought hardest against the change.

None of this is to pretend that the transition is frictionless. Traders worry about deliveries; disabled residents worry about access; commuters worry about time. These concerns are legitimate, and they have answers: timed loading windows, exemptions for blue-badge holders and residents, park-and-ride schemes, and investment in buses that are actually pleasant to use. The cities that have done this well—Ghent, Pontevedra, much of central Copenhagen—did not simply erect bollards and walk away. They planned, consulted and compensated.

What they understood is that a historic centre is not a thoroughfare with old buildings attached. It is a place with a character to protect and a life to sustain. Allowing cars to dominate it is a habit, not a necessity—and habits can be broken. The mayors who break this one will be remembered for it.

title: legislative bill text|an act requiring disclosure of data breaches within 72 hours
text:
Be it enacted by the Legislature of the State of [State]:

SECTION 1. SHORT NAME.
This Act may be cited as the Data Breach Accountability and Notification Act.

SECTION 2. LEGISLATIVE FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.
(a) The Legislature finds that personal information collected and maintained by public and private entities is increasingly vulnerable to unauthorized acquisition, and that delayed detection and disclosure of security breaches substantially increase the risk of identity theft, financial fraud, and other harms to residents of this State.
(b) The purpose of this Act is to establish a uniform, expedited timeline for notification of data breaches, to ensure that affected individuals and appropriate state authorities receive timely and accurate information, and to promote accountability in the handling of personal information.

SECTION 3. DEFINITIONS.
As used in this Act:
(a) "Personal information" means an individual's first name or first initial and last name in combination with any one or more of the following data elements, when either the name or the data elements are not encrypted or redacted: social security number; driver's license or state identification card number; financial account number or credit or debit card number; medical or health insurance information; biometric data; or a user name or email address in combination with a password or security question that permits access to an online account.
(b) "Data breach" means the unauthorized acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of personal information that compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of that information, excluding good-faith acquisition by an employee or agent of the entity if the information is not used or subject to further unauthorized disclosure.
(c) "Entity" means any person, business, governmental body, or third-party service provider that owns, licenses, or maintains personal information of residents of this State.
(d) "Notice" means written or electronic communication to an affected individual, or to the designated state authority where individual notice is not feasible.

SECTION 4. NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS.
(a) An entity that discovers or is notified of a data breach shall provide notice of the breach to each affected resident of this State without unreasonable delay and in no event later than seventy-two (72) hours after the entity discovers the breach, unless the entity determines that the breach does not create a reasonable risk of harm to the affected individuals. Any determination of no reasonable risk shall be documented in writing and retained for a period of not less than five (5) years.
(b) In addition to individual notice, the entity shall notify the designated state authority within seventy-two (72) hours of discovery. The notification shall include, to the extent known: the date and nature of the breach; the categories of personal information involved; the number of affected residents; the measures taken to contain the breach; and contact information for the entity's representative.
(c) An entity that is required to notify more than five hundred (500) residents as a result of a single breach shall also provide notice to the designated state authority in the manner prescribed by regulation.
(d) Notice to individuals shall be clear, conspicuous, and written in plain language, and shall describe the breach, the categories of information involved, the steps affected individuals should take to protect themselves, and the entity's contact information. Notice may be provided by electronic means if the individual has consented to receive communications electronically and the notice is reasonably likely to be received.
(e) A third-party service provider that experiences a breach shall notify the entity on whose behalf it maintains the data within twenty-four (24) hours of discovery. The entity shall then comply with the timelines in this section.

SECTION 5. DELAYS FOR LAW ENFORCEMENT.
An entity may delay notification otherwise required by this Act if a law enforcement agency determines that notification would impede a criminal investigation. Any such delay shall be documented in writing, shall be limited to the period reasonably necessary, and shall not exceed thirty (30) days absent written extension by the law enforcement agency.

SECTION 6. ENFORCEMENT AND PENALTIES.
(a) The designated state authority may investigate violations of this Act and may impose civil penalties of not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000) per day for each day notification is delayed beyond the seventy-two-hour period, up to a maximum of one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) per breach.
(b) The designated state authority may bring an action to enjoin violations and to recover penalties and costs under this section.
(c) A violation of this Act constitutes an unfair or deceptive act or practice under the consumer protection laws of this State.

SECTION 7. SEVERABILITY.
If any provision of this Act or its application is held invalid, the remainder of the Act and its application to other persons or circumstances shall not be affected.

SECTION 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act takes effect one hundred eighty (180) days after enactment.

title: encyclopedia article|the life and career of a nineteenth-century railway engineer
text:
Robert Stephenson (1803–1859) was a British civil engineer and locomotive designer whose work on railways, bridges, and locomotives made him one of the central figures of the nineteenth-century railway age. The only son of George Stephenson, the pioneering railway engineer, he combined technical innovation with large-scale project management and helped establish the railway as the defining technology of the Industrial Revolution.

Robert Stephenson was born on 16 October 1803 in Willington Quay, near Newcastle upon Tyne. His formal education was modest, but his father ensured that he received practical training and, later, a period of study at the University of Edinburgh. In 1821 he assisted his father in surveying the proposed Stockton and Darlington Railway, and in 1823 he became managing partner of Robert Stephenson and Company, the locomotive works founded in Newcastle. The firm quickly gained prominence, producing locomotives for early railways in Britain and abroad.

His reputation as a locomotive engineer was established with the Rocket, which he designed and which won the Rainhill Trials of 1829. The locomotive's multi-tubular boiler and improved blast pipe made it far more efficient than its competitors, and its success secured the Stephenson approach as the standard for steam traction. Robert Stephenson subsequently supplied locomotives to the Liverpool and Manchester Railway and to lines in continental Europe and North America, and his designs influenced locomotive practice for decades.

After the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830, Stephenson turned increasingly to civil engineering. He served as engineer for several major lines, including the London and Birmingham Railway, one of the most ambitious projects of the 1830s. The line required extensive cuttings, tunnels, and viaducts, and its completion in 1838 demonstrated that railways could be built through difficult terrain on a large scale. His later railway work included the Newcastle and Berwick line and consultations on routes in Europe and Egypt.

Stephenson is perhaps best remembered for his bridges. The High Level Bridge at Newcastle upon Tyne, completed in 1849, carried road and rail traffic on two decks and remains in use. The Britannia Bridge across the Menai Strait in Wales, completed in 1850, was a pioneering wrought-iron tubular bridge designed to carry the Chester and Holyhead Railway. Its construction, involving the floating and lifting of enormous iron tubes, was a celebrated engineering feat. The Conway Bridge employed a similar tubular design.

Stephenson also played a significant role in the broader professionalisation of engineering. He served as president of the Institution of Civil Engineers and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. He sat in the House of Commons from 1847 until his death, though he rarely spoke in Parliament. His advice was sought on railway schemes in Britain and overseas, and he mentored a generation of engineers.

Robert Stephenson died on 12 October 1859 at his home in London and was buried in Westminster Abbey. His career spanned the transition from experimental locomotive traction to mature railway infrastructure, and his work on locomotives, railways, and bridges left a lasting mark on nineteenth-century transport. He is remembered as one of the foremost engineers of his age, whose achievements helped shape the modern railway system.

title: NGO policy brief|improving childhood nutrition in rural Kenya
text:
POLICY BRIEF
To: Ministry of Health, Division of Nutrition and Dietetics; County Health Executives, Kitui and Kilifi
From: Executive Director, Tumaini Nutrition Trust
Date: 14 March 2025
Re: Scaling up the Malezi Bora nutrition model in ASAL counties — evidence and recommendations

---

The problem

Four years after the launch of the Kenya Nutrition Action Plan (2023–2027), stunting among children under five in Kitui County still sits at 31.4 per cent, against a national average of 18 per cent. In Kilifi, the figure is 29.8 per cent (KDHS 2022). These are not abstract statistics. In the villages where Tumaini Nutrition Trust works — from Mwingi North to Ganze — they translate into children who will start Class One shorter, sicker and more likely to drop out than their peers in Nairobi.

The drivers are well documented: diets heavy in maize and ugali with little dietary diversity, late introduction of complementary foods, and a shortage of frontline health workers. Kitui has one nutritionist per 42,000 people; the WHO benchmark is one per 5,000. Only 38 per cent of health facilities in the two counties offer full community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) services.

What we tested

Between January 2022 and December 2024, Tumaini ran the Malezi Bora pilot across 24 community health units in Mwingi North and Kaloleni sub-counties, reaching 8,340 children under five and 3,100 pregnant and lactating women. The model had three components:

1. Mother-to-mother support groups, facilitated by trained community health promoters (CHPs), meeting fortnightly to demonstrate affordable local recipes — sorghum porridge fortified with amaranth and groundnut paste, termite-flour biscuits during the hunger gap.
2. A simplified mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) screening protocol run by CHPs, with referrals to 11 link facilities.
3. Market vouchers of KES 1,200 per month, redeemable for eggs, milk, greens and small fish at 34 participating local traders, targeted at households with children identified as moderately malnourished.

Results

An endline survey of 1,900 households (February 2025) found:

- Stunting in the pilot cohort fell from 30.1 per cent to 22.6 per cent — a 7.5-point reduction in 36 months.
- Minimum acceptable diet (MAD) adherence rose from 21 per cent to 54 per cent.
- CHP screening detected 612 cases of severe acute malnutrition that would otherwise have gone unreferred; 91 per cent were treated successfully at link facilities.
- Cost per child reached: KES 2,850 per year, roughly one-fifth the cost of facility-based therapeutic care for a single SAM episode.

The voucher component proved the most contested and the most effective: traders reported a 40 per cent rise in egg and milk sales, and focus groups in Ganze showed fathers increasingly involved in food purchasing decisions.

Recommendations

1. Ring-fence KES 180 million in the FY2025/26 supplementary budget to extend Malezi Bora to 60 additional community health units in Kitui, Kilifi and Tana River, prioritising wards with stunting above 28 per cent.
2. Formalise the CHP MUAC protocol within the Community Health Services framework, with a stipend of KES 3,000 per month and refresher training every six months.
3. Integrate the voucher scheme into the Hunger Safety Net Programme, converting one-off distributions into monthly nutrition-linked transfers during the January–April lean season.
4. Commission an independent costing study by September 2025 to inform a national scale-up business case.

We are available to brief the Division at its earliest convenience.
