title: encyclopedia article|the history of a small coastal town in Maine
text:
The History of Havenport, Maine

Havenport is a small coastal town located in Hancock County, Maine, situated at the mouth of the Wescott River where it empties into Penobscot Bay. With a year-round population of approximately 1,200 residents, the town has preserved much of its historic character while adapting to the economic realities of the modern Maine coast. Its history reflects the broader patterns of settlement, maritime commerce, and seasonal tourism that have shaped many communities along the northeastern seaboard.

The area that would become Havenport was originally inhabited by the Penobscot people, who maintained seasonal fishing camps along the sheltered coves of the bay. European settlement began in 1762, when a small group of families from Massachusetts, attracted by the protected harbor and abundant timber, established a permanent village on the eastern shore. The town was officially incorporated in 1786 and named Havenport, a reference to the safe anchorage its harbor provided to coastal vessels.

During the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, Havenport developed a diversified maritime economy. Shipbuilding emerged as the town's principal industry, with several yards producing schooners and brigs for the coastal trade. Lumber, lime, and salted fish were exported from the town's wharves to markets in Boston, New York, and the West Indies. By the 1840s, Havenport supported a population of nearly 2,500 and boasted three churches, a grammar school, and a weekly newspaper. The prosperity of this period is still visible in the Greek Revival and Federal-style houses that line the town's Main Street.

The second half of the nineteenth century brought significant change. The decline of wooden shipbuilding, the rise of rail transportation, and the depletion of nearby forests eroded the town's commercial base. A devastating fire in 1871 destroyed much of the waterfront district, and many families migrated westward in search of opportunity. By 1900, the population had fallen below 1,000, and Havenport seemed destined to follow numerous other Maine coastal villages into quiet obscurity.

The twentieth century, however, brought renewal through tourism. Beginning in the 1890s, wealthy families from Philadelphia and New York began summering in Havenport, drawn by its cool climate and picturesque setting. Several grand hotels and numerous summer cottages were constructed along the shore. The arrival of the automobile and, later, improved highways made the town accessible to a broader visiting public. Commercial fishing, particularly lobster trapping, also remained an important part of the local economy throughout this period.

In the postwar decades, Havenport balanced its traditional fishing industry with a growing reliance on seasonal tourism and, increasingly, on retirees who chose to make the town their permanent home. The establishment of a historic district in 1978 helped preserve the architectural heritage of the town center, and the Havenport Historical Society, founded in 1952, maintains a museum documenting the community's maritime past.

Today, Havenport remains a small but vital community. Its working harbor still accommodates a fleet of lobster boats, while its restored downtown attracts visitors throughout the summer months. The town's history, marked by cycles of prosperity and decline, illustrates the resilience of Maine's coastal communities and their continuing ability to adapt to changing economic circumstances while preserving a distinctive sense of place.

title: NGO policy brief|improving childhood nutrition in rural Kenya
text:
POLICY BRIEF
To: Ministry of Health, Division of Nutrition and Dietetics; County Health Executives, Kitui and Kilifi
From: Executive Director, Tumaini Child Nutrition Trust
Date: 14 March 2025
Re: Scaling up community-based nutrition in rural Kenya: lessons from Kitui and Kilifi

The problem

Kenya has cut under-five stunting from 35 per cent in 2008 to 18 per cent under the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS), but the national figure conceals a stubborn rural gap. In Kitui County, stunting still stands at 31 per cent; in Kilifi, 26 per cent. Only 42 per cent of children aged 6–23 months in Kitui meet the minimum acceptable diet, against a national average of 52 per cent. These deficits are not random: they track drought cycles, distance to health facilities and the opportunity cost of a mother's time.

What we found

Between January 2023 and December 2024, Tumaini Child Nutrition Trust ran a community-based pilot in 24 villages across Mwingi Central (Kitui) and Ganze (Kilifi), reaching 3,180 children under five and 2,140 pregnant and lactating women. The model was deliberately low-tech: 96 community health promoters (CHPs) recruited from their own villages, equipped with mid-upper arm circumference tapes, counselling flip-charts in Kikamba and Giriama, and a modest monthly stipend of KSh 8,000.

Results, verified by an endline survey conducted with the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) in November 2024:

- Stunting among children under two fell from 29 per cent to 21 per cent in pilot villages, against a 3-point fall in comparison villages.
- Exclusive breastfeeding to six months rose from 48 per cent to 71 per cent.
- The share of households using at least four food groups daily increased from 34 per cent to 58 per cent.
- Cost per child reached: approximately KSh 4,300 per year — roughly one-fifth of the cost of treating a single severe acute malnutrition case in hospital.

The single biggest driver of change was not the food supplement. It was the CHP visit itself: households receiving at least two home visits per month saw twice the dietary diversity gains of those receiving one. Fathers' participation, encouraged through baraza sessions, was associated with a 14-point rise in household dietary diversity.

Recommendations

1. Institutionalise the CHP cadre within county nutrition budgets. The pilot's CHPs operated on donor funding due to end in June 2025. Kitui and Kilifi should absorb at least 60 CHPs each into their 2025/26 budgets, at an estimated KSh 96 million combined — less than 0.4 per cent of each county's health allocation.

2. Fund the Malezi Bora counselling package at scale. The flip-chart and recipe booklet developed under this pilot should be adopted by the Division of Nutrition and Dietetics and printed for all 47 counties. Printing costs are modest; adaptation costs are not.

3. Tie nutrition-sensitive agriculture to the CHP network. County agriculture departments should prioritise kitchen-garden inputs and drought-tolerant seed (amaranth, cowpea, orange-fleshed sweet potato) to households flagged by CHPs as having low dietary diversity, rather than distributing inputs by ward uniformly.

4. Protect the gains during drought. During the 2022 drought, CHP visits in Ganze fell by half as households migrated. Counties should pre-position supplementary food and maintain CHP stipends through emergency periods, when the returns to counselling are highest.

The ask

We request a meeting with the Division of Nutrition and Dietetics before 30 April 2025 to discuss adoption of the Malezi Bora package and a joint funding proposal to the World Bank's Kenya Nutrition and Social Protection Programme. The evidence base is ready; the question is whether the financing follows.

*Contact: Grace Wanjiru Mwangi, Executive Director, Tumaini Child Nutrition Trust, Nairobi. Full endline report available on request.*

title: medical patient information leaflet|managing type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise
text:
Managing Type 2 Diabetes Through Diet and Exercise

Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition in which the level of glucose (sugar) in your blood becomes too high. It develops when your body does not produce enough insulin, or when the insulin it produces does not work effectively. While medication is often part of treatment, the way you eat and the amount you move can have a substantial effect on your blood glucose levels, your weight, and your overall risk of complications. For many people, these changes are as important as any prescription.

Diet

There is no single diet that suits everyone with type 2 diabetes, but the principles are consistent. Aim to eat regular meals, avoid skipping meals, and keep portion sizes steady from day to day; this helps prevent swings in blood glucose. Carbohydrates have the greatest effect on blood sugar, so it is worth paying particular attention to them. Choose wholegrain varieties of bread, rice, and pasta, and favour carbohydrates that release energy slowly. Sugary drinks, sweets, and refined snacks are best kept to a minimum.

A diet rich in vegetables, pulses, nuts, and oily fish is generally recommended, and has benefits for heart health as well as glucose control. Some people find that reducing carbohydrate intake helps them manage their levels; if you wish to try this, discuss it with your diabetes team first, particularly if you take insulin or tablets that can cause low blood sugar. Alcohol should be limited, and you should never drink on an empty stomach if you are taking certain diabetes medicines.

Exercise

Physical activity makes your body more sensitive to insulin, so glucose is cleared from the blood more effectively. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity each week — enough to raise your heart rate and make you breathe harder while still able to hold a conversation. Brisk walking, cycling, swimming, and gardening all count. Activity can be accumulated in short sessions; ten minutes three times a day is as valid as one longer session.

In addition, try to do something to build strength, such as carrying shopping, using resistance bands, or body-weight exercises, on two or more days a week. If you have not been active for some time, start gradually and build up. If you have heart disease, foot problems, or eye changes associated with diabetes, check with your GP or diabetes nurse before beginning a new exercise programme.

Practical points

Check your feet after exercise, as reduced sensation can allow small injuries to go unnoticed. Keep water to hand, and carry a source of fast-acting sugar if you take medication that can cause hypoglycaemia. Your diet and activity levels should be reviewed at your routine diabetes appointments, alongside your HbA1c, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Small, sustained changes are more effective than sudden drastic ones, and support from your diabetes team is available if you need it.

title: wire news story|a central bank holds interest rates steady amid slowing inflation
text:
Central Bank Holds Interest Rates Steady Amid Slowing Inflation

WASHINGTON, March 18 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged, holding the target range at 4.25 percent to 4.50 percent, as policymakers noted that inflation has continued to ease while the labor market remains resilient.

The decision, approved unanimously by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), marked the second consecutive meeting at which the central bank left rates untouched, following a series of cuts last year that lowered borrowing costs by a full percentage point.

In a statement issued after the two-day policy meeting, the committee said that recent indicators suggest economic activity has continued to expand at a moderate pace. Job gains have remained solid, and the unemployment rate has stayed low, the statement said, while inflation has moved closer to the committee's 2 percent longer-run objective, though it remains somewhat elevated.

The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose 2.6 percent in January from a year earlier, down from 2.9 percent in December and well below the peak of 7.2 percent recorded in mid-2022. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, stood at 2.8 percent, continuing a gradual downward trend.

"The committee judges that the risks to achieving its employment and inflation goals are roughly in balance," the statement said. "The economic outlook is uncertain, and the committee is attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate."

Speaking at a press conference following the announcement, Fed Chair Jerome Powell said the central bank was in no hurry to adjust policy, describing the current stance as "well positioned" to respond to evolving economic conditions. He said further progress on inflation would be needed before additional rate reductions could be considered.

"We don't need to be in a rush," Powell said. "We can wait for greater clarity, and we are prepared to respond appropriately if the economy evolves in a way that requires it."

Powell also acknowledged that uncertainty surrounding trade policy and fiscal measures had complicated the outlook, though he declined to speculate on their likely impact. "We are monitoring developments closely," he said.

Financial markets showed little reaction to the decision, which had been widely anticipated. U.S. stocks were modestly higher in afternoon trading, while Treasury yields edged lower. According to CME Group data, investors are pricing in roughly a 60 percent probability of a quarter-point rate cut at the Fed's June meeting.

Economists offered mixed views on the path ahead. Some analysts said the pause was prudent given the gradual cooling of price pressures, while others warned that holding rates at restrictive levels for too long could weigh on growth.

"The Fed has bought itself time, but the window for further easing may narrow if inflation proves stickier than expected," said Sarah Lin, chief economist at a New York-based research firm.

The Fed also released updated economic projections, which showed that most officials expect two rate cuts this year, unchanged from their December forecast. Policymakers projected inflation would end the year at 2.4 percent, slightly higher than earlier estimates, and that the unemployment rate would rise modestly to 4.3 percent.

The committee is scheduled to meet next in early May.

title: press release|a university announces a new research centre for battery technology
text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact: Sarah Jenkins, Director of Media Relations
Phone: +44 (0)20 7946 0123
Email: s.jenkins@northgate.ac.uk

Northgate University Launches £12M Centre for Next-Generation Electrochemistry

LONDON — 14 May 2024 — Northgate University today announced the establishment of the Northgate Centre for Advanced Electrochemistry (NCAGE), a £12 million research facility dedicated to developing the next generation of solid-state battery technology. The Centre, which will officially open its doors on 1 September 2024, aims to bridge the gap between laboratory-scale innovation and commercial manufacturing.

The funding package comprises a £7 million grant from the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) and a £5 million capital investment from Northgate University. The facility will be housed within the University’s existing Science and Innovation Park, occupying 1,200 square metres of refurbished laboratory space on the second floor of the Hargreaves Building.

Professor Alistair Vance, formerly of the Cavendish Laboratory at Cambridge, has been appointed as the Centre’s inaugural Director. Vance brings with him a team of 14 postdoctoral researchers and will oversee the recruitment of an additional 10 PhD students over the next three years. His research into ceramic electrolytes has already yielded two patents, which will form the basis of the Centre’s initial workstreams.

“The gap between a promising coin cell in a lab and a viable electric vehicle battery is enormous,” said Professor Vance. “NCAGE exists to close that gap. We are not just looking at chemistry; we are looking at manufacturing tolerances, thermal runaway mitigation, and the economics of scaling up. If we cannot make it at volume, we have not solved the problem.”

The Centre’s research will focus on three primary areas: sulfide-based solid electrolytes, lithium-metal anode interfaces, and high-throughput manufacturing techniques for thin-film battery components. Industrial partners include Jaguar Land Rover, which will provide £1.5 million in matched funding and access to testing facilities at its Whitley engineering centre, and Oxford-based materials firm Nexeon.

Dr. Helena Marsh, Head of Battery Systems at Jaguar Land Rover, noted that the partnership is designed to shorten the timeline from discovery to deployment. “We need solid-state cells that can survive 1,000 charge cycles at automotive scale,” Marsh said. “Having a dedicated facility that understands our validation requirements from day one is a significant advantage.”

The Centre will also run a public lecture series and an annual open day for local schools, aiming to address the skills shortage in battery engineering. The first cohort of PhD students will begin in January 2025.

Construction on the laboratory fit-out began in March and is scheduled for completion in August. The official opening ceremony will take place on 12 September 2024, with a keynote address from Dame Judith Hackitt.

About Northgate University
Founded in 1964, Northgate University is a research-intensive institution with a focus on engineering, applied sciences, and health. It has an annual research income of £85 million and maintains partnerships with over 200 industrial organisations.

About the EPSRC
The Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council is the UK’s main agency for funding research in engineering and the physical sciences, investing approximately £800 million annually.

title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Two Days in Lisbon on a Budget

Lisbon has acquired a reputation as one of Western Europe's more affordable capitals, but the visitor who arrives without a plan will find that reputation tested quickly. The city rewards those who move deliberately: eating where residents eat, riding the clanking trams rather than taxis, and treating the city's steep hills as part of the experience rather than an obstacle to be paid around. What follows is a route for two days that keeps costs modest without reducing Lisbon to a checklist.

Day one: Alfama and the riverfront

Begin in Alfama, the oldest quarter, where narrow streets climb from the river toward the castle. The Castelo de São Jorge charges admission, but the Miradouro de Santa Luzia and the Miradouro das Portas do Sol, a short walk below it, offer comparable views of terracotta roofs and the Tagus for nothing. Wander without a map; getting briefly lost is part of the district's appeal. For lunch, look for a tasca—a small family-run restaurant—serving the daily prato do dia, typically soup, a main of grilled fish or pork, and coffee for around €10. Avoid the restaurants clustering on the main tourist thoroughfares, where prices double and quality suffers.

In the afternoon, take tram 28 (a single fare loaded onto a reusable Viva Viagem card is substantially cheaper than a day pass bought on board) toward Graça, or simply walk. Ride it early or late to avoid the crush. Descend to the Baixa and walk the riverfront to Belém if energy permits—the flat riverside path takes roughly an hour—or take a train from Cais do Sodré. In Belém, the Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower are best admired from outside if the budget is tight; the queues and entry fees are considerable. The Pastéis de Belém bakery, however, is worth the modest cost of a custard tart.

Dinner should be seafood in a modest neighbourhood restaurant, with vinho verde by the glass. Expect to eat well for €15–20 per person.

Day two: Bairro Alto, Chiado and LX Factory

Start at the Feira da Ladra, Lisbon's sprawling flea market, held on Tuesdays and Saturdays behind the Panteão Nacional. Even browsers will find the atmosphere worth the visit. Continue downhill through Mouraria, stopping for coffee and a bifana—a pork sandwich—at a counter bar, which should cost no more than €5.

Spend the afternoon in Chiado and Bairro Alto, browsing bookshops and the free-to-enter churches, then walk west to Alcântara's LX Factory, a former industrial complex turned into shops, cafés and murals. It is touristy but pleasant, and entry costs nothing. Return to the centre for sunset at the Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara, where the view over the castle costs nothing but the price of a beer from a nearby kiosk.

Practicalities

Buy a Viva Viagem card at any metro station and load it as you go; single journeys cost around €1.80, and the card itself €0.50. Tap water is drinkable. Many museums are free on Sunday mornings, and the city's hilltop viewpoints—the best value in Lisbon—cost nothing at all.

title: legislative bill summary|a bill to expand tax credits for small businesses that hire apprentices
text:
This bill amends the internal revenue code to expand and enhance the existing work opportunity tax credit specifically for small businesses that hire apprentices in qualified trade and industrial programs. The legislation defines a small business as any employer with 100 or fewer full-time equivalent employees. Under the bill, eligible small businesses may claim a credit equal to 50 percent of the first 12,000 dollars of wages paid to each qualified apprentice during the apprentice's first year of employment, up from the current 40 percent of the first 6,000 dollars. For the second year of employment, the bill establishes a new credit equal to 35 percent of the first 10,000 dollars of wages paid to the same apprentice, a benefit not currently available under existing law. The credit is capped at 6,000 dollars per apprentice in year one and 3,500 dollars in year two, and a small business may claim credits for no more than 15 apprentices in any taxable year.

To qualify, an apprentice must be enrolled in a registered apprenticeship program recognized by the Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency, must be employed in a skilled trade, manufacturing, construction, healthcare, information technology, or energy-related occupation, and must not have been employed by the hiring business during the preceding 12 months. The bill requires that apprentices receive at least 144 hours of related technical instruction annually and 2,000 hours of on-the-job training, consistent with registered apprenticeship standards. Wages must meet or exceed the greater of the federal minimum wage or the state minimum wage, and the business must certify that the apprentice position does not displace any existing employee.

The bill directs the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of Labor, to establish a simplified certification process allowing small businesses to claim the credit on their annual return without pre-approval, subject to subsequent audit. Employers must retain apprenticeship registration records and payroll documentation for four years. The credit is nonrefundable but may be carried forward for up to five taxable years. Small businesses with 25 or fewer employees may elect to receive the credit as a quarterly advance payment against payroll taxes, modeled on the existing employee retention credit advance mechanism, to address cash-flow barriers that disproportionately affect the smallest firms.

The bill appropriates 50 million dollars annually for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 to the Department of Labor for grants to states to expand apprenticeship registration capacity and to conduct outreach to small businesses in underrepresented industries and rural areas. It also requires the Comptroller General to submit a report to Congress within three years evaluating credit utilization rates, apprenticeship completion rates, wage outcomes for participants, and any evidence of displacement or credit stacking abuse, with recommendations for program improvement.

The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates the credit expansion will reduce federal revenue by approximately 4.2 billion dollars over the 2026 through 2030 period. The bill's stated purposes are to strengthen the skilled trades pipeline, reduce the cost barrier that prevents small businesses from offering apprenticeships, and increase the number of registered apprentices nationally by an estimated 120,000 over five years. The legislation takes effect for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, and the credit provisions sunset for apprentices hired after December 31, 2030, unless extended by subsequent legislation.

title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Two Days in Lisbon Without Blowing the Budget

Lisbon has a happy knack of making frugal travel feel generous. The light does most of the work; your job is to stay out of its way and keep €60–70 a day in your pocket.

Day one: Alfama and the river

Start at Confeitaria Nacional on Praça da Figueira, trading since 1829. A *pastel de nata* and a *bica* at the counter costs about €2.20 — cheaper standing than seated, as everywhere in town. From there, walk to Martim Moniz and ride the famous Tram 28 — but board at the terminus before 9am, because by 10 it's a sardine tin with a queue. A single ticket bought on board is €3.10; better, load a Viva Viagem card at any metro machine (€0.50 for the card) and top up with a €6.40 24-hour pass covering metro, tram, bus and funiculars.

Ride the 28 to Portas do Sol, then wander down through Alfama's lanes to the Feira da Ladra, Lisbon's flea market, which runs Tuesdays and Saturdays on Campo de Santa Clara. Lunch on a *bifana* (€3–4) from a tasca near the market. Skip the €10 entry to the Castelo de São Jorge and instead take the free terrace at Miradouro de Santa Luzia for the same view of terracotta roofs and the Tejo.

In the afternoon, catch the Cais do Sodré–Cacilhas ferry (€1.55 each way with your card) for a cheap river crossing and a look back at the city. Dinner: Time Out Market is fun but pricey; instead head to Ramiro's neighbour, the unassuming *cervejaria* Bitoque on Rua da Alegria, where a steak-and-egg *bitoque* with a glass of house red runs about €12.

Day two: Belém and Bairro Alto

Take tram 15 from Praça da Figueira to Belém early — the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos cloisters (€12) open at 9:30 and the queue triples by 11. If the €12 stings, the church itself is free. The Pastéis de Belém bakery, operating since 1837, sells its warm custard tarts for €1.40 each; eat them in the park opposite rather than paying for table service.

The Museu Nacional dos Coches (€8) is a curiosity worth an hour, but if you'd rather save, the Torre de Belém exterior and the riverside promenade cost nothing. Return via the LX Factory under the 25 de Abril bridge — free to wander, good for a €4 coffee and a browse.

Spend the evening in Bairro Alto, where bars are tiny, beer is €1.50–2, and the street is the living room. Finish with a *ginjinha* (€1.50) from a hole-in-the-wall kiosk on Rua das Portas de Santo Antão.

Sleep cheap: hostels around Rossio and Intendente run €25–35 for a dorm in spring; a private double at a *pensão* in Alfama can be had for €60. Book direct and ask about the Lisboa Card only if you plan heavy museum-hopping — for two days of trams and tarts, the Viva Viagem pass wins every time.

title: government audit report|oversight of veterans' disability claim processing times
text:
Section 3: Oversight of Disability Claim Processing Times

3.1 Scope and Methodology

This section examines the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA) administration of disability compensation claims, with particular focus on the Veterans Benefits Administration's (VBA) performance in meeting processing-time targets established under the Veterans Appeals Improvement and Modernization Act of 2017 and subsequent departmental strategic plans. The audit team reviewed claims data for fiscal years 2021 through 2024, interviewed officials at four regional processing offices and VBA central office, and analyzed a statistical sample of 385 claims files. We assessed compliance with internal processing benchmarks and evaluated the adequacy of VBA's performance monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

3.2 Background

The VA's disability compensation program serves approximately 6.3 million veterans, with VBA adjudicating roughly 1.7 million claims annually in recent years. Departmental policy sets a target of 125 days for completion of initial disability claims, a benchmark first established in 2010. VBA reports processing times through its Monday Morning Workload Report and the Veterans Benefits Management System (VBMS), which serves as the system of record for claims tracking. The agency has publicly committed to reducing the average days to complete (ADC) for all claim types while maintaining accuracy rates above 90 percent.

3.3 Findings

3.3.1 Processing Times Exceed Targets for Certain Claim Categories

Our analysis determined that while VBA met its 125-day target for initial claims in the aggregate during fiscal year 2024, performance varied considerably by claim category. Average processing times for claims requiring medical examinations exceeded the target in three of four quarters reviewed, ranging from 128 to 141 days. Appeals remanded by the Board of Veterans' Appeals averaged 187 days for completion, well beyond the 125-day benchmark. Supplemental claims averaged 119 days, within target, though the 90th percentile exceeded 200 days.

3.3.2 Accuracy and Timeliness Trade-offs Not Transparently Reported

VBA's public reporting presents processing times and accuracy rates as separate metrics without disclosing the relationship between them. Our file review identified 47 claims (12.2 percent of the sample) in which expedited processing appeared correlated with elevated error rates, particularly in cases involving complex medical evidence. Departmental guidance does not require analysis of this relationship, and VBA officials acknowledged that no systematic review of timeliness-accuracy trade-offs is conducted. Without such analysis, Congress and the public lack a complete picture of program performance.

3.3.3 Workload Management Practices Vary by Regional Office

We found significant variation in workload management practices across the four regional offices visited. Two offices employed systematic triage protocols that prioritized claims by complexity and age, while two relied primarily on first-in, first-out processing. The offices with triage protocols completed older claims more rapidly but reported higher rates of development requests—follow-up actions to obtain evidence—which extended overall processing time for affected claims. VBA central office has not issued government-wide guidance on workload prioritization, leaving practices to regional discretion.

3.3.4 Performance Monitoring Lacks Leading Indicators

VBA's performance dashboard emphasizes lagging indicators, such as completed claims and average days to complete, but contains limited leading indicators that might foreshadow processing delays. For example, the dashboard does not track the volume of claims awaiting medical examinations or the age distribution of pending development requests. Officials in two regional offices stated that they maintain such data locally but do not report it upward. The absence of leading indicators limits VBA's ability to anticipate and mitigate backlogs before they materialize.

3.4 Conclusion

VBA has generally met aggregate processing-time targets but does not consistently meet them across all claim categories, does not transparently report the relationship between timeliness and accuracy, permits variation in workload management practices without assessing their effects, and relies on lagging rather than leading performance indicators. These conditions limit the department's ability to provide Congress and the public with a complete and accurate assessment of claims processing performance.

3.5 Recommendations

We recommend that the Under Secretary for Benefits: (1) develop and publish processing-time targets by claim category and report performance against them quarterly; (2) analyze and disclose the relationship between processing speed and accuracy in annual reporting; (3) issue guidance on workload prioritization and assess the effects of differing practices; and (4) incorporate leading indicators, including pending examination volumes and development-request age distributions, into the VBA performance dashboard.

---

*Note: This is a drafted illustrative section. Agency responses were not available at the time of drafting and would ordinarily be summarized in the final report.*

title: encyclopedia article|a species of freshwater turtle and its conservation status
text:
The European pond turtle (Emys orbicularis) is a medium-sized freshwater turtle native to Europe, western Asia, and parts of North Africa. It is the only member of the genus Emys found in Europe and is among the most widely distributed freshwater turtles on the continent, though its populations are fragmented and in decline across much of its range. The species is characterized by a dark olive to blackish carapace, often speckled with fine yellow dots, and soft parts of the body marked with yellow spots. Adults typically reach a carapace length of 12 to 25 centimeters, with females generally larger than males. The species is long-lived, with individuals in the wild capable of exceeding 60 years of age, and it exhibits delayed sexual maturity, slow reproduction, and high adult survival, life-history traits that make populations slow to recover from losses.

The European pond turtle occupies a wide variety of slow-moving and standing freshwater habitats, including ponds, lakes, marshes, oxbows, ditches, and the quiet backwaters of rivers. It prefers water bodies with abundant aquatic vegetation, muddy bottoms, and accessible sunny banks for basking, which is essential for thermoregulation and shell health. The species is carnivorous and opportunistic, feeding on aquatic insects, larvae, crustaceans, mollusks, amphibians, and carrion, and it occasionally takes plant material. Females leave the water in late spring and early summer to lay clutches of roughly 3 to 16 eggs in sandy or loose soil, often traveling considerable distances from water. Hatchlings may overwinter in the nest and emerge the following spring. Across its range, the species occupies a mosaic of habitats, and population connectivity depends on networks of wetlands and suitable terrestrial nesting sites.

The conservation status of the European pond turtle is a matter of concern throughout its range. Globally, the International Union for Conservation of Nature assesses the species as Near Threatened, reflecting widespread population declines and range contraction, particularly at the northern and western edges of its distribution. In many European countries the species is listed as endangered or critically endangered at the national level, and it is protected under the Bern Convention and the European Union Habitats Directive, which requires member states to designate protected areas and safeguard breeding and resting sites. The primary threats are habitat loss and degradation, driven by wetland drainage, river channelization, agricultural intensification, urbanization, and the conversion of nesting banks for development or recreation. Fragmentation isolates populations, reducing genetic exchange and making local extinctions less likely to be reversed by natural recolonization. Additional pressures include road mortality, particularly of egg-laying females, disturbance of nesting sites, predation of nests and hatchlings by foxes, raccoons, and other subsidized predators, and collection for the pet trade. Climate change poses a longer-term risk by altering wetland hydrology and shifting suitable thermal conditions, and the species' temperature-dependent sex determination may make populations vulnerable to warming.

Conservation efforts focus on protecting and restoring wetland complexes, maintaining open sunny nesting banks, and reducing road mortality through fencing and underpasses at known crossing points. Captive breeding and head-start programs have been used to reinforce depleted populations, particularly in northern Europe, and reintroduction projects have been undertaken in several countries. Monitoring programs track population trends and reproductive success, while public awareness campaigns discourage the collection of wild turtles and the release of captive or non-native turtles into the wild. Because the species is long-lived and slow to reproduce, conservation success requires long-term commitment and landscape-scale management of interconnected wetland and terrestrial habitats. The European pond turtle thus serves as an indicator of wetland health and as a flagship for freshwater conservation in Europe.

text:
Flooding has forced hundreds of families from their homes in a Welsh valley after torrential rain caused rivers to burst their banks, with emergency services warning that further disruption is likely in the coming days.

Residents in the affected communities were evacuated overnight as water levels rose rapidly, submerging roads and sweeping away vehicles. Local authorities described the situation as unprecedented, with some areas experiencing their worst flooding in more than three decades.

The Welsh Ambulance Service and fire crews worked through the night to rescue people trapped in their properties, using boats and specialist equipment to reach vulnerable residents. Rest centres have been established in local schools and community halls, where evacuated families are being provided with shelter, hot food and support.

One resident, who asked not to be named, said the water had risen with alarming speed. "We had maybe twenty minutes to gather what we could before it was knee-deep in the hallway," she said. "We have never seen anything like it."

Natural Resources Wales, the body responsible for flood defences, said river levels had peaked at record highs in several locations. A spokesperson confirmed that flood warnings remained in force across the valley and urged people to avoid travelling unless absolutely necessary.

The First Minister expressed sympathy for those affected and chaired an emergency meeting of the Welsh Government's resilience committee. Ministers pledged that additional resources would be deployed to support recovery efforts, and that a review of flood defences in the region would be conducted once the immediate crisis had passed.

Forecasters warned that further heavy rain is expected over the next forty-eight hours, compounding the difficulties faced by emergency responders. The Met Office has issued an amber warning for the region, advising that communities should prepare for possible further flooding.

Local councillors said the scale of the evacuation had placed significant strain on public services, but praised the response of emergency workers, volunteers and neighbouring authorities who had offered assistance.

The leader of the county council said: "Our priority is the safety and wellbeing of residents. We are working closely with partners to ensure that everyone who has been displaced has somewhere safe to stay, and we will do everything possible to help our communities recover."

The flooding is the latest in a series of extreme weather events to hit Wales in recent years, and comes amid growing concern about the impact of climate change on vulnerable communities. Environmental groups argued that investment in flood defences and natural flood management schemes should be accelerated.

As water levels begin to recede in some areas, attention is turning to the long task of clean-up and damage assessment. Insurance companies have reported a sharp rise in claims, and many families face the prospect of being unable to return to their homes for several weeks.

For now, the valley remains largely cut off in places, with emergency services continuing to monitor the situation. Officials have warned that the full extent of the damage may not be known until the floodwaters have fully subsided.

title: environmental impact statement|a proposed wind farm off the coast of New Jersey
text:
Section 4.3: Avian and Bat Ecology

The proposed wind energy facility, sited approximately 12 nautical miles off the coast of New Jersey, intersects a region of recognized ecological significance. The lease area lies within the Atlantic Flyway, a principal migratory corridor through which millions of birds and bats travel annually between breeding grounds in the northeastern United States and Canada and wintering habitats to the south. This section assesses the potential effects of construction, operation, and decommissioning on avian and bat populations, drawing on two years of site-specific radar and acoustic survey data, regional migration records, and the published literature on offshore wind facilities in European and North American waters.

Baseline surveys recorded 147 bird species within or adjacent to the lease area, including federally listed species such as the piping plover (*Charadrius melodus*), red knot (*Calidris canutus rufa*), and roseate tern (*Sterna dougallii*). Radar data indicate that migratory passage is concentrated during spring and autumn, with peak nocturnal passage rates in late April and mid-September. Notably, the majority of migratory flight occurs above the rotor-swept zone, a pattern consistent with observations at operational facilities in the mid-Atlantic. Seven bat species were detected acoustically, with the eastern red bat (*Lasiurus borealis*) and hoary bat (*Lasiurus cinereus*) accounting for the majority of passes; offshore bat activity was low relative to mainland reference sites but exhibited seasonal peaks coinciding with autumn migration.

Collision risk represents the most direct potential impact. Using a collision-risk model parameterized with site-specific passage rates, turbine dimensions, and avoidance probabilities derived from European post-construction monitoring, the predicted annual collision mortality is estimated at 4.2 to 11.6 birds per turbine and fewer than 1.1 bats per turbine, with the upper bounds reflecting conservative avoidance assumptions. These estimates carry substantial uncertainty, and post-construction fatality monitoring—adapted for offshore conditions through the use of trained detection dogs, acoustic sensors, and systematic carcass surveys—will be required to validate model predictions. Importantly, estimated mortality must be evaluated against population-level thresholds rather than considered in isolation; for common species, predicted losses are expected to be demographically negligible, while for listed species even small additions to baseline mortality warrant scrutiny.

Indirect effects merit comparable attention. Construction noise, vessel traffic, and pile-driving activity may displace birds from foraging and resting habitat, particularly during the sensitive wintering period for sea ducks and loons. Behavioral disturbance is expected to be localized and temporary, ceasing with the completion of installation. Operational effects include potential barrier effects on migratory flight paths—though evidence from existing facilities suggests most migrants readily route around arrays—and altered foraging conditions within the lease area. Decommissioning will produce effects similar in kind and lesser in magnitude than those of construction.

Cumulative impacts require regional coordination. Several wind energy areas are under consideration along the Atlantic Outer Continental Shelf, and the aggregate effect of multiple facilities on flyway populations is not yet well understood. The applicant will participate in the regional science framework convened by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management to support cumulative assessment.

Mitigation measures include seasonal restrictions on pile-driving during peak migration where practicable, implementation of a collision-risk minimization protocol informed by post-construction monitoring, and funding of regional avian research. With these measures, and subject to the monitoring contingencies described in Section 6.1, the proposed action is not anticipated to result in significant adverse effects on avian or bat populations. Residual uncertainty is acknowledged and will be addressed through adaptive management.

title: legislative bill summary|a bill to expand tax credits for small businesses that hire apprentices
text:
This bill, cited as the Small Business Apprenticeship Tax Credit Expansion Act, amends the Internal Revenue Code to broaden and enhance existing tax incentives for qualifying small businesses that hire apprentices in registered apprenticeship programs. The legislation is intended to address persistent skills gaps in skilled trades, manufacturing, healthcare support, and information technology by lowering the cost of apprenticeship training for employers with fewer than 100 full-time employees.

The centerpiece of the bill is an increase in the per-apprentice credit. Under current law, eligible employers may claim a credit of $2,000 per qualifying apprentice for the first year of the apprenticeship. The bill raises this amount to $4,000 for the first year and creates a new $2,500 credit for the second year of a qualifying apprenticeship, subject to the apprentice remaining in the program and meeting satisfactory progress benchmarks established by the registered program sponsor. A supplemental credit of $1,000 is available for apprentices from designated opportunity zones, apprentices who are veterans, and apprentices under age 25 who are entering the workforce for the first time.

Eligibility is expanded in several respects. The gross receipts ceiling for qualifying small businesses rises from $50 million to $75 million, indexed annually for inflation, and the full-time employee cap increases from 100 to 150. The bill also permits eligible employers to claim the credit for apprentices enrolled in pre-apprenticeship programs recognized by the Department of Labor, provided the apprentice transitions into a registered program within 12 months. Part-time apprentices working at least 20 hours per week become eligible for a prorated credit equal to half the standard amount.

The bill simplifies administration for small employers. It directs the Secretary of the Treasury to develop a streamlined certification process allowing employers to claim the credit based on documentation from the registered apprenticeship sponsor rather than requiring independent verification of each apprentice's hours. The credit becomes refundable for employers with 25 or fewer employees, enabling startups and very small firms with limited tax liability to benefit. Unused credits may be carried forward for up to five years.

To guard against abuse, the bill requires recapture of credits if an apprentice leaves the program within six months without good cause, and it prohibits claiming the credit for apprentices who are immediate family members of more than 50 percent owners. The bill also excludes employers who have reduced their overall workforce by more than 10 percent in the preceding year, preventing firms from substituting apprentices for existing employees.

The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates the bill will reduce federal revenue by approximately $1.8 billion over ten years. The bill appropriates $25 million annually to the Department of Labor for program outreach, sponsor capacity grants, and a public database of registered apprenticeship opportunities. Reporting requirements direct the Treasury and Labor Departments to submit a joint evaluation to Congress after three years assessing take-up rates, completion rates, wage outcomes for apprentices, and the credit's effect on hiring among small businesses. The bill takes effect for taxable years beginning after December 31 of the year of enactment.

Statement of Need

Our community has undergone significant demographic and economic change over the past several decades. Longtime residents possess invaluable knowledge of local history, including the closure of local industries, waves of immigration, the evolution of neighborhood institutions, and everyday life in earlier eras. Much of this history exists only in personal memory and has never been systematically recorded. Without deliberate intervention, these stories risk being lost forever. At the same time, many residents, particularly younger people and newcomers, express a strong desire to understand the community's past and to connect with their neighbors across generational and cultural divides. The library, as a trusted public institution, is uniquely positioned to bridge these gaps.

Project Goals and Objectives

The project has three primary goals: first, to record and preserve at least forty oral history interviews with residents representing diverse ages, backgrounds, and neighborhoods; second, to train community volunteers in interview techniques, ethical consent practices, and audio recording; and third, to make the collected stories publicly accessible through the library's digital repository and through public listening events.

Activities and Timeline

During the first quarter, project staff will finalize interview protocols, purchase recording equipment, and recruit volunteers through library programming and community partners. A professional oral historian will conduct two training workshops covering interview methodology, consent procedures, and equipment use. In the second and third quarters, trained volunteers will conduct interviews, with the project coordinator providing ongoing support and quality review. Each participant will sign a consent form specifying how their recording may be used. In the fourth quarter, recordings will be edited, catalogued, and uploaded to the library's digital archive. The project will conclude with two public listening events and a printed booklet featuring edited excerpts.

Evaluation

Success will be measured by the number of completed interviews, volunteer retention and satisfaction, archive usage statistics, and attendance at public events. Participants will complete brief feedback surveys, and the project coordinator will submit a final report documenting outcomes and lessons learned.

Budget Summary

Funds are requested for recording equipment, honoraria for the professional trainer, volunteer training materials, digital storage and hosting, printing of the commemorative booklet, and light refreshments for public events. The library will contribute staff time and meeting space as in-kind support.

Organizational Capacity

[Name of Public Library] has served the community for [number] years and offers established programming, digital infrastructure, and strong relationships with local schools, historical societies, and community organizations. The project will be managed by [Name/Title], who brings relevant experience in public programming and project coordination.

Conclusion

Voices of Our Neighborhood will transform the library into an active center for community memory and connection. By capturing stories that would otherwise go unheard, the project will create a lasting public resource and strengthen the bonds between generations of residents. We respectfully request the committee's support for this initiative.

title: environmental impact statement|a proposed wind farm off the coast of New Jersey
text:
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STATEMENT — EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Project: Atlantic Horizon Offshore Wind Farm
Location: Federal waters approximately 14 miles southeast of Long Beach Island, Ocean County, New Jersey
Prepared for: New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, Office of Clean Energy
Date of Issue: March 14, 2025
Lead Consultant: Barnegat Environmental Associates, LLC, Trenton, NJ

---

1. Project Description

Atlantic Horizon Wind, LLC proposes to construct and operate a 1,100-megawatt offshore wind facility consisting of 74 turbines (15 MW class) mounted on monopile foundations, arrayed across a 68,000-acre lease area (OCS-A 0539) in the New York Bight. Power would come ashore via two 220 kV submarine export cables making landfall at the former Oyster Creek generating station site in Lacey Township, with an onshore switching station and interconnection to the existing 230 kV Barnegat substation. Construction is scheduled to begin in the second quarter of 2027, with commercial operation targeted for December 2029.

2. Affected Environment

The lease area lies in water depths of 95 to 130 feet, overlaying sandy substrates with scattered gravel and shell hash. Benthic surveys conducted between April and October 2024 recorded 41 infaunal taxa, dominated by polychaetes and amphipods. The site intersects a documented surfclam bed of moderate density and seasonal habitat for black sea bass and summer flounder. Baseline acoustic monitoring (2023–2024) identified presence of North Atlantic right whales, humpback whales, and bottlenose dolphins, primarily during the November–April migration window. The nearest shoreline is Barnegat Light, roughly 14 statute miles west-northwest; the viewshed analysis indicates turbines would subtend approximately 0.6 degrees of horizontal arc from the Barnegat Lighthouse deck at typical visibility.

3. Potential Impacts and Mitigation

*Benthic and Fisheries:* Monopile installation would permanently convert approximately 52 acres of benthic habitat and temporarily disturb another 310 acres. Pile-driving noise is expected to exceed the 160 dB re 1 µPa injury threshold absent attenuation. The applicant has committed to a double big-bubble curtain system, soft-start procedures, and a 90-minute clearance zone monitored by two dedicated Protected Species Observers. Seasonal restrictions would prohibit impact pile driving from December 1 through April 30 to protect migrating right whales.

*Avian:* Radar studies at the nearby Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge recorded 12,400 bird crossings per season, chiefly red-throated loons and northern gannets. Collision risk modeling (Band-share, 2024 parameters) predicts 1.8 to 4.1 fatalities per turbine per year under a 12 rotations-per-minute operational cap. Curtailment protocols would be triggered during peak nocturnal migration.

*Visual and Socioeconomic:* Commercial fishing interests in Barnegat Light and Point Pleasant have raised concerns regarding transit corridors; a 1-nautical-mile setback from the surfclam bed has been incorporated. Tourism impact modeling for Long Beach Island projects no measurable decline in seasonal visitation.

4. Cumulative Impacts

Cumulative assessment considered the adjacent Ocean Wind 1 and Atlantic Shores projects. Combined, the three facilities would occupy roughly 4.3 percent of the New York Bight lease blocks. Cumulative pile-driving noise and vessel traffic were modeled under a worst-case concurrent schedule; results suggest temporary displacement, not mortality, for most fish species.

5. Conclusion

With the mitigation measures described — seasonal pile-driving restrictions, noise attenuation, avian curtailment, and fisheries compensation — the proposed action is not anticipated to result in significant adverse impacts to protected species or regional ecosystems. Barnegat Environmental Associates recommends approval subject to the conditions enumerated in Section 7 and a five-year post-construction monitoring program funded by the applicant.

*Prepared by: M. Ellsworth Haines, Lead Environmental Planner, NJ Licensed Site Remediation Professional No. 58214*

title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Day one in Lisbon starts with the famous pastel de nata, and the good news is you do not need to pay tourist prices for one. Skip the long queues at the big name bakeries in Belem and head instead to a neighborhood pastelaria, where a custard tart and a bica, the local espresso, should cost you around two euros total. From there, walk. Lisbon is a city best explored on foot, and the historic center is compact enough that you can cover a lot of ground without touching public transport.

Start in Alfama, the oldest quarter, a maze of steep alleys, tiled facades and laundry lines. Getting lost here is the point. Climb gradually toward the Miradouro de Santa Luzia for free views over the red roofs and the river, then continue up to the castle district. You do not need to pay to enter the castle itself; the surrounding streets and the viewpoints nearby offer just as good a panorama. For lunch, look for a tasca, a small family-run eatery, away from the main squares. A prato do dia, the daily plate, with soup, bread and a drink often costs under ten euros.

In the afternoon, wander down to Baixa and the riverfront, then take the free walk along the water toward Alcantara if you have energy, or simply rest in one of the city's many small parks. As evening comes, head to Bairro Alto, but eat before you go. Dinner in a simple restaurant in the Chiado or Principe Real area will be far cheaper than in the nightlife streets. After dark, Bairro Alto becomes a street party, and the cheapest way to enjoy it is to buy a beer from a small bar or kiosk and drink it outdoors with the crowds, as locals do.

Day two begins early to beat the queues. Take the tram or a short bus ride to Belem, but note that the famous monastery and tower charge entry fees. If your budget is tight, admire the tower from the riverside garden for free and visit the free parts of the waterfront instead. The Monument to the Discoveries and the riverside promenade cost nothing and offer excellent views. Pack a picnic from a supermarket or market before you go; Belem's cafes are pricey.

In the afternoon, ride the historic Tram 28 if you want the experience, though it can be crowded and costs a few euros, or simply walk the route through Graca and Mouraria for free. These neighborhoods are less polished than Alfama but full of character and cheap cafes. Finish your day at a miradouro with a supermarket beer and a view, watching the sun go down over the city.

A few practical tips keep costs down. Buy a rechargeable transit card if you plan several rides; single tickets add up. Eat your main meal at lunch, when restaurants offer better value. Drink the local wine and beer rather than cocktails. And remember that many of Lisbon's best experiences, the viewpoints, the tiled streets, the river, are entirely free. Two days here on a budget is not only possible, it is one of the most enjoyable ways to see the city.

text:
Market Research Report: Consumer Demand for Electric Bicycles in Europe
*Prepared: March 2025 | Reporting Period: FY2024*

Executive Summary

European consumer demand for electric bicycles continued its upward trajectory in 2024, though the pace of growth has moderated from the pandemic-era surge. According to data published by the Confederation of the European Bicycle Industry (CONEBI) in February 2025, e-bike sales across the EU-27 plus the UK reached approximately 5.9 million units in 2024, up 4.2% year-on-year, while total bicycle sales remained flat at around 14.7 million units. E-bikes now account for roughly 40% of all bicycle revenue in the region, a figure that stood below 25% as recently as 2019.

Regional Demand Patterns

Germany remains the largest single market, with the Zweirad-Industrie-Verband (ZIV) reporting 2.1 million e-bikes sold in 2024 and e-bikes comprising 53% of all bicycle sales by volume. France follows, where Union Sport & Cycle recorded 780,000 e-bike units sold, supported by the national *bonus vélo* scheme, which was extended through 2027 under the France 2030 plan. The Netherlands, Belgium, and Austria show the highest per-capita penetration: in Belgium, e-bike share of bicycle sales exceeded 60% in 2024, according to Traxio figures.

Growth is now fastest in the emerging markets of Southern and Eastern Europe. Spain saw e-bike sales rise 19% in 2024 to 310,000 units (AMBE data), while Poland crossed 200,000 units for the first time, driven largely by commuter models priced between €1,200 and €2,000.

Consumer Segments and Motivations

Our survey of 2,400 respondents across six markets (conducted January–February 2025 in partnership with a pan-European panel provider) identifies three dominant buyer profiles. Commuters aged 35–54 represent 46% of purchase intent, citing fuel savings and urban congestion as primary drivers. The 55+ leisure segment accounts for 31%, with comfort and health maintenance ranking above environmental concerns. A younger segment (18–34) is growing quickly, now at 18% of intent, drawn to cargo and gravel e-bikes.

Price sensitivity has sharpened. The average e-bike selling price in Germany fell to €2,350 in 2024 from €2,560 in 2022, per ZIV, reflecting heavy discounting as inventory levels normalized after the 2023 oversupply crisis that hit suppliers including Accell Group and Pierer Mobility.

Barriers and Outlook

Purchase barriers remain consistent: upfront cost (cited by 58% of non-owners), battery range anxiety (34%), and lack of secure parking or charging infrastructure (29%). The EU's revised battery regulation, effective August 2024, adds compliance costs that manufacturers are expected to pass through partially in 2025–2026.

We forecast European e-bike demand to grow at a compound annual rate of 5.5% through 2028, reaching approximately 7.6 million units, with the strongest gains in France, Spain, and Poland. The leasing channel—particularly Germany's *Dienstrad-Leasing* model, which accounted for 38% of ZIV-member sales in 2024—will remain a critical demand driver, alongside municipal incentive programs tied to the EU's Urban Mobility Framework.

title: technical documentation|configuring a home network router for parental controls
text:
Configuring Parental Controls on a Home Router

Parental controls at the router level offer a centralized means of managing internet access across every device on a home network, without the need to install or maintain software on each individual device. Because filtering occurs at the point where the network meets the internet, router-based controls apply uniformly to computers, smartphones, tablets, and gaming consoles alike. This section describes the general procedure for configuring these controls and the principal decisions involved.

 Prerequisites

Before beginning, confirm that the router's administrative interface is accessible. Connect a computer to the network—by Ethernet cable where possible—and navigate to the router's management address, typically printed on a label affixed to the device or documented in the manufacturer's manual. Sign in with administrator credentials. If the router still uses the default password supplied by the manufacturer, change it before proceeding; an unsecured administrative interface exposes every configuration described in this section to alteration by anyone on the network.

It is also advisable to record the router's current settings, either through a built-in backup or export function or by photographing each configuration screen, so that changes can be reversed if necessary.

 Establishing Access Policies

Most consumer routers organize parental controls around user profiles or device groups. Begin by identifying the devices to be managed and assigning them to a profile—for example, one profile for younger children and another for teenagers. Devices not assigned to a profile typically remain unrestricted, so verify that each device appears in the correct group.

Next, define the content restrictions. Routers commonly offer category-based filtering (such as mature content, gambling, or social media), blocklists of specific domains, and safe-search enforcement for major search engines. Select the categories appropriate to the household, and add any specific sites to be blocked or permitted. Where the router supports an allowlist mode—blocking everything except approved destinations—consider it for devices used by young children, though this approach requires more ongoing maintenance.

 Scheduling and Time Limits

Time-based controls allow administrators to define when internet access is available. Configure bedtime restrictions to suspend connectivity during overnight hours, and set daily allowances where the router supports cumulative usage limits. Note that scheduled restrictions generally apply to the connection as a whole rather than to individual applications; a device with access during a permitted window can reach any service not otherwise filtered.

 Applying and Verifying Settings

Save the configuration and, where the router offers the option, reboot it to ensure policies take effect. Verification is essential: from a managed device, attempt to reach a blocked category or domain, and confirm that access is refused. Test the schedule by temporarily setting a restriction to begin within a few minutes. Repeat the test on each device class in the household, since filtering behavior can vary between operating systems.

 Limitations and Maintenance

Router-based parental controls are effective but not comprehensive. They do not inspect encrypted traffic in depth, and determined users may circumvent them through cellular data, VPNs, or alternate DNS settings. For this reason, router controls are best treated as one layer within a broader approach that includes device-level settings and direct supervision.

Review the configuration periodically—at minimum every few months and whenever new devices join the network—to confirm that policies remain appropriate and that firmware updates have not altered behavior. Manufacturers occasionally revise filtering categories or interface layouts, so re-verifying blocked content after any firmware upgrade is prudent.

Congressional Research Report

Subject: The History and Current Debate over Agricultural Subsidies

This report provides a historical overview and analysis of the current policy debate surrounding agricultural subsidies in the United States. Agricultural subsidies have been a cornerstone of federal farm policy since the 1930s, designed initially to stabilize farm incomes and ensure a reliable food supply. The debate over their efficacy, equity, and economic impact continues to shape legislative action, most recently in the context of the Farm Bill reauthorization.

The modern era of agricultural subsidies began with the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933, a New Deal response to the Great Depression. The Act introduced price supports and production controls to address severe commodity price collapses and widespread farm foreclosures. Over subsequent decades, the policy framework evolved through various Farm Bills. The 1970s saw a shift toward direct payments, while the 1996 Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform (FAIR) Act sought to decouple subsidies from production decisions. However, subsequent legislation, including the 2002 and 2008 Farm Bills, reintroduced counter-cyclical payments and expanded crop insurance programs. The 2014 and 2018 Farm Bills further consolidated this approach, emphasizing risk management tools like crop insurance and eliminating direct cash payments in favor of price and revenue support programs.

The current debate is characterized by several key tensions. Proponents argue that subsidies are essential for national food security, mitigating the inherent risks of weather, market volatility, and global competition. They contend that these programs stabilize rural economies and ensure a stable supply of affordable food. Crop insurance, in particular, is viewed as a vital risk management tool for producers.

Critics, however, raise significant concerns. Economists often argue that subsidies distort planting decisions, lead to overproduction of certain commodities, and inflate land values, ultimately benefiting large agribusinesses more than small family farms. The distributional equity is a major point of contention, with data consistently showing that the largest farms receive a disproportionate share of payments. Environmental groups criticize subsidies for encouraging monoculture farming and discouraging conservation practices. Furthermore, international trade partners frequently challenge U.S. subsidies at the World Trade Organization, arguing they violate fair trade principles by depressing global prices.

The debate is further complicated by the upcoming 2023 Farm Bill reauthorization. Legislators are grappling with how to balance the safety net for producers against fiscal responsibility, equity concerns, and environmental sustainability. Proposals range from tightening payment limits and means-testing to redirecting funds toward conservation and climate-smart agriculture. The outcome will determine the future structure of the American agricultural safety net.

In conclusion, while agricultural subsidies have a long history rooted in crisis response, the contemporary debate reflects a complex interplay of economic, social, and environmental priorities. The challenge for Congress is to modernize a legacy system to meet the needs of a diverse agricultural sector while addressing broader public concerns regarding equity, trade, and sustainability.

text:
MEMORANDUM

TO: Elena Vasquez, General Counsel
FROM: Daniel Whitcomb, Associate
DATE: March 14, 2025
RE: Enforceability of Non-Compete Clause in Hartwell Employment Agreement

I. Question Presented

Whether the non-compete provision in Section 9(b) of the employment agreement between our client, Nathan Hartwell, and his former employer, Brighthaven Logistics, Inc., is enforceable under the law of the state of Missouri.

II. Short Answer

Probably not, though the outcome is not free from doubt. Missouri courts enforce non-competes only when they protect a legitimate interest and are no broader than necessary to protect that interest. Brighthaven's clause—which bars Hartwell from working for any "competitor" anywhere in the United States for two years—is likely overbroad on both geography and scope. There is a reasonable argument that the court may blue-pencil the clause rather than void it, but as drafted it would probably fail.

III. Facts

Hartwell worked as a regional sales manager for Brighthaven, a St. Louis-based freight brokerage, from March 2019 until he resigned on January 10, 2025. As regional sales manager, Hartwell managed client relationships for accounts in eastern Missouri and southern Illinois, and had access to Brighthaven's pricing models and customer lists.

Section 9(b) of his employment agreement, signed March 4, 2019, provides that for twenty-four months after termination, Hartwell may not "directly or indirectly engage in, own, manage, or be employed by any business that competes with the Company anywhere in the United States." The agreement contains no geographic limitation tied to Hartwell's territory and no carve-out for passive ownership. In February 2025, Hartwell accepted a position as a logistics coordinator with Kestrel Freight Solutions, a small brokerage in Paducah, Kentucky, that occasionally handles shipments originating in Missouri. Brighthaven sent a cease-and-desist letter on February 21, 2025, threatening suit.

IV. Discussion

Missouri law treats non-competes as restraints of trade and construes them narrowly. *Osage Glass, Inc. v. Donovan*, 693 S.W.2d 71 (Mo. 1985), established the governing framework: a covenant is enforceable only if it is necessary to protect a legitimate interest—typically trade secrets or customer contacts—and is reasonable in duration and geographic scope. *Whelan Security Co. v. Kennebrew*, 379 S.W.3d 835 (Mo. 2012), reaffirmed that customer contacts justify a covenant only where the employee's relationships are the "predominant" asset the employer seeks to protect.

Here, duration is defensible; Missouri courts have upheld two-year terms. The problem is geography. In *Schmersahl, Treloar & Co. v. McHugh*, 28 S.W.3d 345 (Mo. App. E.D. 2000), the court refused to enforce a covenant lacking any territorial limit, reasoning that a nationwide bar was unreasonable where the employee's work was confined to a single region. Hartwell's book of business was concentrated in eastern Missouri and southern Illinois, yet Section 9(b) reaches coast to coast. And because Kestrel's Missouri-origin shipments are a small fraction of its business, Brighthaven will struggle to show the Paducah job threatens the interests the covenant purports to protect.

Brighthaven may ask the court to modify the clause under the blue-pencil doctrine. Missouri courts will narrow an overbroad covenant, but only where the modifications are "limited and not extensive." *Johnson v. Medtronic, Inc.*, 365 S.W.3d 226 (Mo. App. E.D. 2012). Rewriting "anywhere in the United States" into a defined regional territory, and redefining "competitor" to exclude a role like Hartwell's current one, may exceed what courts will do. We should anticipate the argument but not count on it.

V. Conclusion

Section 9(b) is vulnerable to challenge, chiefly on geographic breadth. If Brighthaven sues, we should move to dismiss or seek declaratory judgment in St. Louis County Circuit Court promptly, before Kestrel's hiring creates additional friction. Please advise whether you would like a draft complaint prepared this week.

Section 3: Oversight of Disability Claim Processing Timeliness

3.1 Scope and Methodology

This section evaluates the effectiveness of oversight mechanisms governing the timeliness of veterans' disability compensation claim processing within the Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA) for the period beginning October 1, 2021, and ending September 30, 2024. The audit examined whether VBA headquarters and regional offices maintained adequate controls to monitor, measure, and report processing timeliness; whether performance data submitted to oversight bodies were complete and reliable; and whether corrective actions for identified delays were implemented and sustained. Methodologies included review of departmental directives and standard operating procedures; analysis of claims-level data extracted from the Veterans Benefits Management System (VBMS); structured interviews with 47 officials across headquarters, four regional offices, and two oversight entities; and examination of monthly performance reports submitted to the Under Secretary for Benefits and to Congress.

3.2 Summary of Findings

Oversight of claim processing timeliness was partially effective. VBA established measurable timeliness targets and a tiered reporting structure that escalated regional performance deficiencies to headquarters attention. However, the audit identified three material weaknesses that limit the assurance oversight bodies can derive from reported results. First, timeliness metrics excluded certain categories of claims—notably those requiring supplemental development or those returned from appeal—thereby understating the average time veterans waited for a complete decision. Second, regional offices exercised broad discretion in recording claim receipt dates and development actions, introducing inconsistencies that rendered cross-regional comparisons unreliable. Third, corrective action plans for underperforming offices lacked measurable milestones and were not systematically tracked to closure.

3.3 Detailed Observations

*3.3.1 Incomplete Timeliness Metrics.* VBA's primary timeliness measure, the average days to complete, is calculated from a population that excludes claims with certain procedural characteristics. During the audit period, approximately 11 percent of completed claims fell outside the reported metric. Analysis of a statistically valid sample of excluded claims found that their average processing time exceeded that of included claims by 38 days. Consequently, reported averages did not fully reflect the experience of the veteran population, and oversight bodies relying on these figures received an incomplete picture of actual wait times.

*3.3.2 Data Integrity Vulnerabilities.* The audit tested 200 claims across four regional offices and found discrepancies in receipt-date recording for 23 claims (11.5 percent). In nine instances, receipt dates were entered after initial development actions had already occurred, a sequencing inconsistent with VBMS system controls. Interviews with staff attributed inconsistencies to workload pressures and ambiguous guidance on handling mail-dated claims. Because timeliness calculations depend directly on receipt dates, these vulnerabilities undermine confidence in performance data reported upward and to Congress.

*3.3.3 Corrective Action Tracking.* Headquarters required regional offices with sustained performance deficiencies to submit corrective action plans. Of 14 plans reviewed, 11 lacked quantified milestones, and none were subject to systematic follow-up verification. Officials in two regional offices stated that plans were treated as administrative submissions rather than management tools. As a result, the audit could not verify whether any plan produced durable improvement.

3.4 Conclusion

VBA's oversight framework contains the structural elements necessary to monitor processing timeliness, but weaknesses in metric coverage, data integrity, and corrective action follow-through materially diminish its effectiveness. Absent remediation, oversight bodies cannot rely on reported timeliness data as a complete and accurate representation of veterans' experience, and performance deficiencies risk persisting without verified correction.
