text:
OFFICE OF THE INSPECTOR GENERAL
DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
AUDIT REPORT NO. 24-01983-117
DATE: August 14, 2025

SUBJECT: Oversight of Disability Compensation Claim Processing Times at the Veterans Benefits Administration

Executive Summary

The Office of the Inspector General (OIG) conducted an audit of the Veterans Benefits Administration's (VBA) management of disability compensation claim processing times across its 56 regional offices. The audit covered claims adjudicated between October 1, 2023, and March 31, 2025. We found that while VBA reduced the average processing time for initial claims from 124 days to 108 days during this period, the agency's oversight of backlog reduction efforts lacked the data validation needed to confirm reported gains. Additionally, we identified $47.2 million in overtime expenditures at four regional offices that were not supported by documented workload justifications.

Background

As of March 31, 2025, VBA's pending compensation claims inventory stood at 412,600, of which 68,300 (16.6 percent) exceeded 125 days—the threshold VBA uses to define a claim as part of the backlog. The agency's fiscal year 2025 budget included $312 million for claims processing operations, a 9.4 percent increase over FY 2024. The Under Secretary for Benefits, Joshua D. Mercer, has publicly committed to eliminating the backlog by the end of FY 2026.

Findings

*Finding 1: Processing time data reported to Congress was not independently verified.*

VBA's Veterans Benefits Management System (VBMS) generates processing time metrics that are transmitted quarterly to the House and Senate Committees on Veterans' Affairs. We sampled 240 claims across the St. Louis, Winston-Salem, and Oakland regional offices and found that 31 claims (12.9 percent) contained date-stamp errors that understated actual processing time by an average of 19 days. At the Oakland Regional Office, a system migration completed on November 7, 2024, caused 2,140 claims to be logged with a single adjudication date, artificially compressing reported averages for the fourth quarter of FY 2024. VBA's Office of Performance Analysis did not flag the anomaly before the data was reported to Congress on January 15, 2025.

*Finding 2: Overtime spending lacked documented justification.*

Four regional offices—Houston, San Juan, Chicago, and Seattle—incurred a combined $47.2 million in overtime between October 2023 and March 2025. Our review of 180 overtime authorization requests found that 94 (52.2 percent) lacked the required workload projection or supervisory certification mandated by VBA Directive 20-19. The Houston Regional Office alone accounted for $18.6 million, with no documented justification for 61 of 75 authorization requests reviewed. VBA's Office of Resource Management did not conduct the semiannual overtime reviews required under the directive for either FY 2024 or the first half of FY 2025.

*Finding 3: Contract medical examiner delays were not tracked.*

Approximately 34 percent of claims requiring a Compensation and Pension (C&P) examination in our sample experienced delays exceeding 60 days in scheduling. VBA does not track examination scheduling timelines by contractor, despite paying $1.1 billion to three contractors—QTC Medical Services, Loyal Source Government Services, and OptumServe—in FY 2024. Regional office staff at three of five sites visited reported relying on informal email inquiries rather than system-generated status reports.

Recommendations

We recommend that the Under Secretary for Benefits: (1) implement a data validation protocol for VBMS processing time metrics before quarterly reporting to Congress; (2) enforce Directive 20-19 overtime documentation requirements and conduct the overdue semiannual reviews; and (3) require contractors to report examination scheduling timelines through a standardized interface by March 31, 2026.

Management Response

VBA concurred with all three recommendations. Mr. Mercer's response, dated July 28, 2025, committed to implementing the data validation protocol by December 2025 and to completing the overdue overtime reviews by October 31, 2025. VBA did not provide a completion date for the contractor tracking recommendation.

*— Report prepared by: Karen L. Whitfield, Director, Benefits Inspection Division; reviewed by: Anthony R. Delgado, Deputy Inspector General for Audits and Evaluations.*

title: court opinion summary|a dispute over a contractor's failure to complete a home renovation
text:
In the Matter of the Arbitration between Harlan and Reyes

Contractor’s Failure to Complete Renovation Warrants Damages, but Not the Full Relief Sought

*Superior Court, Civil Division. Before Judge Marta Ellison.*

This dispute arises from a home renovation gone badly awry. In 2022, the plaintiffs, Priya and Daniel Harlan, engaged the defendant, Reyes Construction LLC, to undertake a substantial renovation of their residence. The project, which encompassed a kitchen gut, the addition of a primary suite, and structural work on a rear extension, was priced at $412,000 under a fixed-fee contract that specified a completion date of March 31, 2023. The work did not proceed as planned. By the fall of 2023, the project remained unfinished, the parties’ relationship had collapsed, and the Harlans had terminated the agreement. They now seek damages for breach of contract, while the defendant counterclaims for unpaid invoices and for sums it says it is owed for work performed outside the original scope.

The court finds, as a threshold matter, that Reyes Construction breached the contract. The evidence at trial established a pattern of delay that the defendant attributed to material shortages and municipal permitting, but which the record shows was at least equally the product of the contractor’s own disorganization. The defendant’s project manager left the firm in May 2023 and was not replaced for nearly two months; during that interval, subcontractors arrived to find no supervision and, in several instances, no instructions. The court is unpersuaded by the defendant’s argument that the Harlans’ insistence on design changes excused performance. The changes were modest, were documented in signed change orders, and did not account for the roughly seven months of delay that accumulated. A contractor who undertakes a fixed-fee project assumes the risk of ordinary scheduling difficulty, and the defendant has not shown that the delays it encountered were beyond its control.

The more difficult question is the measure of damages. The Harlans ask for the full cost of completion—approximately $168,000, based on a replacement contractor’s bid—together with consequential damages for the eleven months they were obliged to rent alternative accommodation. The court awards the cost of completion. That measure is the ordinary rule where a contractor abandons a project, and the replacement bid submitted by the plaintiffs bears sufficient indicia of reliability: it was prepared by a licensed contractor, itemized by trade, and subjected to meaningful cross-examination. The court declines, however, to award the full sum claimed for rental expenses. The Harlans lived in the residence for part of the relevant period and would have incurred some housing cost in any event; the court awards the differential between their ordinary mortgage and carrying costs and the rent they actually paid, a sum of $31,400.

The court also rejects the defendant’s counterclaim for unpaid invoices. The invoices in question were rendered after the Harlans’ termination of the contract and, in several instances, bill for work that was either incomplete or defective. The defendant’s claim for extras is likewise unavailing: the alleged oral modifications were never reduced to writing as the contract required, and the testimony offered in support of them was, on the whole, vague as to both scope and price.

The court enters judgment for the plaintiffs in the amount of $199,400, together with prejudgment interest and costs. Counsel for the plaintiffs shall submit a proposed judgment consistent with this opinion within fourteen days.

title: medical patient information leaflet|managing type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise
text:
Patient Information Leaflet: Managing Type 2 Diabetes with Diet and Exercise

This leaflet provides general information for patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes about how diet and physical activity can help control blood glucose levels. It does not replace the advice of your doctor, diabetes nurse or dietitian. Please discuss any changes to your routine with your healthcare team.

Understanding type 2 diabetes

Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body does not produce enough insulin or when insulin does not work effectively. As a result, glucose remains in the blood instead of being used for energy. Over time, high blood glucose can damage the heart, blood vessels, eyes, kidneys and nerves. Healthy eating and regular exercise are central to managing the condition and reducing the risk of complications.

Healthy eating

There is no single diet that suits everyone with type 2 diabetes. The aim is to eat a balanced, varied diet, maintain a healthy weight and keep blood glucose levels stable. The following principles are recommended.

Eat regular meals. Spreading food evenly throughout the day, rather than skipping meals, helps prevent large swings in blood glucose. Breakfast should not be missed.

Choose high-fibre, starchy foods. Wholegrain bread, brown rice, wholewheat pasta, oats, beans and lentils release energy slowly and help you feel full for longer. Aim to include a portion with each meal.

Limit sugary foods and drinks. Sugary drinks, sweets, cakes and biscuits raise blood glucose quickly and provide little nutritional value. Water, sugar-free drinks or unsweetened tea and coffee are better choices.

Reduce salt and saturated fat. Too much salt can raise blood pressure, and saturated fat increases cholesterol. Choose lean meat, fish, low-fat dairy products and healthy oils such as olive or rapeseed oil.

Eat plenty of fruit and vegetables. Aim for at least five portions a day. Fruit contains natural sugar, so it is best eaten whole rather than as juice, and portions should be spread across the day.

Watch portion sizes. Eating smaller portions and using smaller plates can help with weight control. If you are overweight, losing even a modest amount of weight can significantly improve blood glucose control.

Alcohol should be consumed in moderation and never on an empty stomach, as it can cause hypoglycaemia, particularly if you take certain diabetes medicines.

Physical activity

Regular exercise helps the body use insulin more effectively and lowers blood glucose. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, such as brisk walking, cycling or swimming, spread over several days. In addition, muscle-strengthening activities, such as carrying shopping or gardening, should be performed twice a week.

Start gradually if you are not currently active. Short sessions of ten minutes, built up over time, are effective. Choose activities you enjoy, as this makes it easier to keep them up. Wear comfortable shoes and check your feet after exercise, as people with diabetes are more prone to foot problems.

Before starting a new exercise programme, speak to your healthcare team, especially if you take insulin or medicines that can cause low blood glucose. You may need to check your blood glucose before, during or after activity and adjust your medication or snack accordingly.

Monitoring and support

Check your blood glucose as advised and attend your regular diabetes reviews. Keep a record of your meals and activity if this helps you identify patterns. Small, consistent changes are more sustainable than strict short-term diets. Your diabetes team can provide individual advice and support.

When to seek help

Contact your doctor or diabetes nurse if you experience frequent low blood glucose, persistent high readings, unexplained weight loss, or if you have any concerns about your diet or exercise plan.

This leaflet is for information only and should not replace professional medical advice.

title: encyclopedia article|the history of a small coastal town in Maine
text:
Castine, Maine

Castine is a town in Hancock County, Maine, situated on the eastern shore of Penobscot Bay at the mouth of the Penobscot River. The community occupies a peninsula of roughly 7.8 square miles and had a population of 1,320 at the 2020 census. Despite its modest size, Castine holds a place of unusual prominence in the early colonial and military history of northeastern North America, having changed hands among European powers more often than perhaps any other settlement in New England.

French explorer Samuel de Champlain visited the site in 1604 and named it Pentagouet, after a local Abenaki term. French traders established a seasonal post there in the 1610s, and in 1628 the Plymouth Colony granted the peninsula to a group of English investors, though effective English settlement did not take hold for decades. The French built Fort Pentagouet in 1635; Baron Jean-Vincent d'Abbadie de Saint-Castin, a French officer, took command in 1670 and married into the Penobscot nation, and the point overlooking the harbor still bears his name.

The town's fortunes turned on its position. In 1779, during the American Revolution, a British force under General Francis McLean began fortifying the peninsula, prompting the disastrous Penobscot Expedition—the worst naval defeat in American history until Pearl Harbor—in which a fleet commanded by Commodore Dudley Saltonstall and ground forces under Brigadier General Solomon Lovell failed to dislodge the British and lost some two dozen vessels. The British held Castine until the war's end and renamed it New Ireland, briefly encouraging Loyalist settlement.

The pattern repeated in the War of 1812. A British squadron under Sir Edward Pulteney captured the town in September 1814, and the occupiers again made it a haven for refugees and disaffected Americans, even publishing a newspaper, the *Castine Journal*. The Treaty of Ghent returned the territory to the United States in 1815.

Castine's postwar economy rested on shipping, lumber, and the sea. The town incorporated as Castine in 1796, and by the 1830s its harbor supported a merchant fleet active in the West Indies trade. The Maine Maritime Academy, founded in 1941, occupies the site of the former Eastern State Normal School and remains the town's largest employer and defining institution.

The peninsula's layers of occupation—French, Dutch, English, American—have left an archaeological record of exceptional density. Excavations conducted since the 1970s, notably by the Maine State Museum and later by archaeologists working with the Castine Research Corporation, uncovered the remains of Fort Pentagouet and evidence of seventeenth-century colonial life that reshaped scholarly understanding of the region's contested frontier. The town's historic district, listed on the National Register of Historic Places, preserves a streetscape largely built between 1790 and 1860, including the 1790 John Perkins House and the 1796 Wilson Museum, both maintained by the Castine Historical Society.

title: encyclopedia article|the history of a small coastal town in Maine
text:
History of Havenport, Maine

The area now comprising Havenport was inhabited for millennia by the Wabanaki peoples, particularly bands of the Penobscot, who maintained seasonal fishing and hunting camps along the sheltered inlet. European settlement began tentatively in the 1630s, when fishermen from the Massachusetts Bay Colony established rudimentary shore stations for drying cod. Permanent occupation, however, was delayed by the region's contested position on the frontier between English and French spheres of influence; the settlement was abandoned twice during the colonial wars of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries.

Havenport was incorporated as a town in 1762, its boundaries carved from the larger neighboring township of Wescott. The name, chosen by the first proprietors, reflected both the harbor's natural advantages and a measure of promotional ambition. The early economy rested on subsistence farming, lumber, and the coastal trade in salt fish, which was shipped to the West Indies and exchanged for molasses and rum. Shipbuilding emerged as a significant secondary industry in the 1790s, and by 1810 the town supported two yards producing schooners for the coasting trade.

The town's fortunes rose sharply in the second quarter of the nineteenth century. Havenport's deep and well-protected harbor made it a natural point of call for vessels engaged in the burgeoning trade in Maine lumber and lime, and the 1830s saw the construction of three wharves, a customs house, and the granite block warehouses that still line Water Street. The population peaked at approximately 2,400 in 1850, a figure the town has never since approached. Incorporation as a city was briefly debated in the 1850s but rejected by town meeting.

The decades after the Civil War brought sustained decline. The diversion of coastal shipping to rail, the exhaustion of nearby timber stands, and the collapse of the West Indies trade eroded Havenport's commercial base. The great fire of 1871, which destroyed eleven buildings on the eastern wharves, proved a decisive blow to the waterfront economy. Emigration to the industrial cities of Massachusetts and to the emerging mill towns of the interior reduced the population by nearly half between 1860 and 1900. Through this period the town subsisted on small-scale fishing, subsistence agriculture, and the summer trade, as visitors from Boston and New York began to discover the Maine coast.

The twentieth century saw Havenport reorient itself toward seasonal tourism and, later, retirement. The arrival of the Portland and Coastal Railroad spur in 1898 and the construction of a small hotel on the bluff above the harbor established the pattern that persists today: a summer population several times the year-round figure, a stock of nineteenth-century houses increasingly converted to seasonal use, and a local economy anchored in hospitality, boatbuilding, and the care of the elderly. The town's historic district, encompassing Water Street and the Federal-style houses of the original proprietors, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. The 2020 census recorded a year-round population of 1,187, a modest increase from the low point of the 1970s and a figure that reflects the town's enduring appeal as a place of quiet, if diminished, consequence.

title: product review|a mid-range noise-cancelling headphone after three months of use
text:
I've been using these mid-range noise-cancelling headphones for about three months now, and I think I've finally got a good handle on what they do well and where they fall short. I bought them primarily for a daily commute that involves a noisy bus ride and a fair amount of walking through a busy city, plus for focus time at a shared office. At this price point, I wasn't expecting flagship-level performance, but I was hoping for solid noise cancellation, decent sound, and reasonable comfort. For the most part, they deliver, with a few caveats worth knowing before you buy.

Let's start with noise cancellation, since that's the headline feature. On the bus, they do a genuinely good job with the low, constant rumble of the engine and road noise. It's not the eerie silence you get from the very top-tier models, but it takes the edge off enough that I can listen at a much lower volume than I used to. Voices and higher-pitched sounds are a different story. They're softened but definitely still audible, so if you're trying to block out a chatty coworker, these will help but won't work miracles. There's also a slight sense of pressure on the ears when the cancellation is at full strength, which I noticed a lot in the first week but have mostly gotten used to since.

Sound quality has been pleasant overall. The bass is present and punchy without being overwhelming, mids are clear enough for podcasts and vocals, and the highs are smooth rather than sharp. They're not the last word in detail, and true audio enthusiasts will probably find them a bit safe-sounding, but for commuting and everyday listening they're easy to live with for hours. Battery life has matched the claims closely; I charge them roughly once a week with about two hours of use a day, and I've never run out unexpectedly. The quick-charge feature has saved me more than once when I forgot to plug them in the night before.

Comfort is where these really shine. The ear cups are soft and the clamping force is gentle, so I can wear them through a full workday without my ears getting hot or my jaw feeling sore. The headband padding is adequate, though I do notice it slightly on longer sessions. They fold up neatly and came with a decent case, which makes them easy to toss in a bag. Build quality feels solid for the price, mostly plastic but with no rattles or creaks so far. The controls are physical buttons rather than touch, which I personally prefer because they work reliably with gloves on and don't misfire when I adjust the headphones.

Now for the frustrations. The microphone is mediocre. People on calls say I sound fine in a quiet room but noticeably muffled outdoors or in the office, and one colleague described me as sounding like I was "in a tunnel." The app is functional but basic, and the transparency mode, while useful, has a faint hiss that's noticeable in quiet environments. Bluetooth connection has been stable overall, but I've had two or three instances of the headphones refusing to pair immediately with my laptop, requiring a restart. Minor, but annoying.

After three months, I'd say these are a sensible buy if you want most of the benefits of noise cancellation without paying flagship prices. They're comfortable, sound good, and handle the daily commute well. Just don't expect silence on the level of premium models, and don't count on them for important calls in loud places. For the money, they've earned their place in my bag every day.

title: legislative bill text|an act requiring disclosure of data breaches within 72 hours
text:
A BILL

To require covered entities to disclose data breaches to affected individuals and the Director of the National Cyber Security Office within 72 hours, and for other purposes.

*Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled,*

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

This Act may be cited as the “Timely Breach Disclosure Act of 2025.”

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.

In this Act:

(1) COVERED ENTITY.—The term “covered entity” means any person or organization that, in the ordinary course of business, collects, processes, or stores the personal data of more than 5,000 individuals residing in the United States, including corporations, nonprofit organizations, and state and local government agencies, but excluding sole proprietorships with fewer than 10 employees.

(2) PERSONAL DATA.—The term “personal data” means a individual’s name in combination with any one or more of the following: Social Security number; driver’s license or state identification number; financial account number together with any security code; medical or health insurance information; biometric data; or a username together with a password or other credential permitting access to an online account.

(3) DATA BREACH.—The term “data breach” means the unauthorized acquisition, access, disclosure, or destruction of personal data maintained by a covered entity, excluding an incident that a reasonable investigation determines is unlikely to result in harm to affected individuals.

(4) DIRECTOR.—The term “Director” means the Director of the National Cyber Security Office established under section 4.

SEC. 3. DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS.

(a) NOTICE TO AFFECTED INDIVIDUALS.—A covered entity that experiences a data breach shall notify each affected individual in writing, by mail and, where an electronic mail address is on file, by electronic mail, not later than 72 hours after the entity confirms the breach. The notice shall describe, in plain language, the categories of personal data involved, the date or estimated date of the breach, the steps the entity has taken to mitigate harm, and a toll-free telephone number and email address at which affected individuals may obtain additional information at no cost.

(b) NOTICE TO THE DIRECTOR.—A covered entity shall submit a report of the breach to the Director not later than 72 hours after confirmation. The report shall state the number of individuals affected, the nature and scope of the breach, the identity of the suspected perpetrator if known, and the entity’s remediation plan.

(c) DELAY FOR LAW ENFORCEMENT.—If a federal law enforcement agency determines that notification would impede a criminal investigation, the agency may, in a written directive delivered to the covered entity, delay notification for a period not to exceed 30 days. Any such directive shall be reported to the Director within 24 hours of issuance.

(d) THIRD-PARTY VENDORS.—A vendor that experiences a breach affecting data it maintains on behalf of a covered entity shall notify that covered entity not later than 24 hours after confirmation, and the covered entity shall bear the notification obligations under this section.

SEC. 4. ENFORCEMENT.

(a) CIVIL PENALTIES.—The Director may assess a civil penalty of not more than $25,000 per day for each day a violation of section 3 continues, up to a maximum of $5,000,000 per breach. In setting the penalty, the Director shall consider the entity’s size, the sensitivity of the data, and whether the entity self-reported in good faith.

(b) PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION.—An individual harmed by a violation of this Act may bring a civil action for actual damages, injunctive relief, and reasonable attorney’s fees.

SEC. 5. EFFECTIVE DATE.

This Act shall take effect on January 1, 2026, and shall apply to any data breach confirmed on or after that date.

title: BBC-style news article|a football club fined after fans invade the pitch
text:
Football Club Fined £250,000 After Fans Invade Pitch in Promotion Celebrations

By Sports Correspondent

A football club has been fined £250,000 and warned over its future conduct after supporters invaded the pitch during celebrations following a decisive end-of-season match, in an incident that has prompted fresh debate about safety and stewarding in the English game.

The club, which has not been named for legal reasons while an appeal is considered, was charged with failing to ensure orderly conduct after several hundred fans entered the field of play at the final whistle. The match, a victory that secured promotion, had been attended by more than 26,000 spectators, including around 3,000 visiting supporters.

An independent regulatory commission, convened by the Football Association, heard that the incursion began within seconds of the referee blowing for full time. Stewards were described as being “overwhelmed” by the volume of supporters moving towards the pitch, and it took approximately 14 minutes for the playing surface to be cleared. No serious injuries were reported, although the commission was told that two stewards suffered minor injuries and a number of supporters required treatment for crush-related complaints at the perimeter fences.

In its written findings, the commission said the club had “failed to take all reasonable steps to prevent spectators from entering the field of play” and that the scale of the incursion had created a “foreseeable risk of harm”. It acknowledged, however, that the club had cooperated fully with the investigation and had already commissioned an independent review of its matchday operations.

The fine is among the larger penalties imposed at this level in recent seasons, and reflects what the commission described as the “aggravating factor” of a previous warning issued to the club 18 months ago following a similar, smaller-scale incident. Half of the sum will be suspended for two years, conditional on the club implementing a series of safety improvements agreed with the relevant authorities.

Speaking after the ruling, a club spokesperson said: “We accept the commission’s decision and apologise unreservedly to those affected. The scenes at full time were a source of great concern to the club, and we are determined to ensure they are not repeated. We have already begun a thorough review of our stewarding, ticketing and crowd-management arrangements, and we will implement its recommendations in full before the start of next season.”

The incident has renewed scrutiny of pitch invasions, which have become more frequent as clubs mark promotions, relegations and title successes. While such scenes are often portrayed as harmless expressions of joy, safety officials have repeatedly warned of the risks posed to players, match officials and opposing supporters. In recent years, several players have been confronted or assaulted during invasions, and the governing bodies have issued guidance urging clubs to adopt stricter preventive measures.

The Football Supporters’ Association said it understood the “raw emotion” of such moments but urged fans to respect the boundaries of the pitch. “Celebrations belong in the stands, however momentous the occasion,” a spokesperson said. “Clubs and supporters alike have a responsibility to ensure that the day is remembered for the right reasons.”

The club has until the end of the month to lodge an appeal. In the meantime, its safety certificate will be reviewed by the local authority, and additional conditions are expected to be attached to its licence for the coming season, including enhanced segregation and a revised stewarding plan for fixtures identified as high-risk.

The commission’s decision is likely to be studied closely by other clubs, many of whom will now review their own protocols ahead of a summer in which several promotion and relegation issues are expected to be decided in front of capacity crowds. For the club concerned, the immediate priority is clear: to ensure that the exuberance of its supporters does not again place the safety of those on and around the pitch at risk.

title: government audit report|delays and cost overruns in a federal broadband grant program
text:
The Office of Inspector General has completed an audit of the Broadband Infrastructure Expansion Grant Program administered by the Office of Rural Connectivity. The audit examined program performance from fiscal year 2021 through fiscal year 2024, focusing on schedule adherence and budgetary controls for 42 grants totaling approximately $1.8 billion. The objective was to determine whether grant recipients and program officials effectively managed project timelines and costs, and whether oversight controls were adequate to identify and address emerging risks.

The audit found significant and widespread delays. Of the 42 grants reviewed, 34, or 81 percent, had experienced schedule slippage, with an average delay of 14 months beyond the original completion date. Eleven grants were delayed by more than two years. As of the audit cutoff date, only nine projects had reached substantial completion, and three had not yet begun construction despite having received funds more than 18 months earlier. Delays stemmed from multiple causes, including incomplete environmental and permitting reviews at the time of award, inaccurate applicant cost estimates, workforce shortages among contractors in rural areas, and supply chain disruptions affecting fiber optic equipment. Program officials did not consistently track milestone data, and required quarterly progress reports were missing or submitted late for 19 of the 42 grants.

Cost overruns were similarly pervasive. Twenty-seven grants, or 64 percent, exceeded their approved budgets, with overruns ranging from 8 percent to 61 percent of the original award amount. Total reported cost growth across the portfolio exceeded $214 million. In several instances, recipients requested supplemental funding or revised budgets without adequate documentation justifying the changes. The audit identified weak controls over budget modification requests: 12 of 18 modification requests reviewed lacked required cost analyses, and approvers did not consistently verify that revised budgets remained within program cost-effectiveness thresholds. Additionally, the program office did not maintain a consolidated record of cost overruns, limiting its ability to identify systemic problems or report accurately to Congress.

Oversight and monitoring weaknesses contributed to both problems. The program office conducted only 15 site visits during the audit period, despite awarding 42 grants, and relied primarily on self-reported data from recipients. The audit also found that program officials did not use available project management tools to flag at-risk projects, and communication with recipients about performance issues was inconsistently documented. These gaps allowed delays and overruns to persist without timely corrective action.

The audit makes several recommendations. First, the Office of Rural Connectivity should implement a standardized milestone tracking system and require timely submission of progress reports as a condition of continued funding. Second, the office should strengthen controls over budget modifications, including mandatory cost analyses and documented approvals. Third, it should establish a consolidated cost overrun reporting mechanism and use it to inform congressional reporting and risk assessments. Fourth, the office should conduct risk-based site visits and develop a formal process for issuing corrective action plans to underperforming recipients. Finally, the office should incorporate lessons learned into future grant design, including more rigorous pre-award reviews of applicant capacity and permitting readiness.

Management generally concurred with the findings and recommendations and indicated that corrective actions are underway, including development of a new grants management tracking system and updated monitoring procedures. The Office of Inspector General will follow up on implementation during the next audit cycle.

title: legislative bill summary|a bill to expand tax credits for small businesses that hire apprentices
text:
This bill, cited as the Small Business Apprenticeship Tax Credit Expansion Act, amends the Internal Revenue Code to broaden and enhance the existing work opportunity tax credit specifically for small businesses that hire apprentices in qualified skilled trades and technical fields. The legislation aims to address persistent labor shortages in skilled occupations, encourage private-sector investment in workforce development, and reduce the financial barriers that small employers face when establishing or expanding apprenticeship programs.

Under the bill, a qualified small business is defined as an employer with no more than 500 full-time equivalent employees. The credit is available for each eligible apprentice hired after the enactment date and applies to apprentices enrolled in a registered apprenticeship program approved by the Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency. The credit amount is set at 50 percent of the apprentice's first-year wages, up to 8,000 dollars per apprentice, and 40 percent of second-year wages, up to 6,000 dollars per apprentice. This represents a substantial increase over the current credit structure, which caps first-year benefits at 25 percent of wages up to 6,000 dollars.

The bill expands eligibility by removing the prior requirement that apprentices be from targeted disadvantaged groups, instead making the credit available for any apprentice who meets program enrollment and age requirements. It also introduces an additional 1,500 dollar credit for small businesses that hire apprentices from underrepresented populations in their trade, including veterans, individuals transitioning from incarceration, and residents of economically distressed communities. Furthermore, the bill provides a supplemental credit of up to 2,000 dollars per apprentice for small businesses that cover the cost of related technical instruction, tools, or required safety equipment.

To prevent abuse, the bill includes integrity provisions. Employers must retain documentation of apprenticeship program registration, wage records, and hours worked. The credit is disallowed for apprentices who are rehired within twelve months following prior employment with the same employer, and employers may not claim the credit for apprentices who replace striking workers or are employed in positions that displace existing employees. The Treasury Department is directed to issue guidance within 180 days of enactment and to coordinate with the Department of Labor to establish a simplified verification process for small businesses.

The bill also authorizes a pilot program within the Small Business Administration to provide technical assistance grants to small businesses seeking to establish registered apprenticeship programs, with priority given to businesses in rural areas and industries facing critical skill shortages. A total of 25 million dollars is appropriated for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030 for this purpose.

The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates that the bill will reduce federal revenue by approximately 1.2 billion dollars over the ten-year period from 2026 to 2035. The bill includes offset provisions by extending certain customs user fees and adjusting reporting requirements for large partnerships. The legislation is not expected to impose significant new regulatory burdens on small businesses, as the Treasury Department is instructed to minimize paperwork through electronic certification options.

The bill will take effect for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. It is expected to be referred to the Committee on Finance and the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship for consideration. Supporters argue the bill will strengthen the skilled workforce pipeline and reduce reliance on public assistance, while critics raise concerns about revenue cost and the need for stronger safeguards against program abuse.

title: congressional research report|the history and current debate over agricultural subsidies
text:
Section 2: Historical Evolution of Federal Agricultural Subsidy Policy

Federal intervention in American agriculture predates the Republic itself, but the modern architecture of agricultural subsidies took shape during the New Deal. The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933, enacted amid collapsing commodity prices and widespread farm foreclosures, introduced the core mechanism that would define subsidy policy for decades: direct federal payments to farmers in exchange for supply management. By restricting acreage and compensating growers for idled land, the federal government sought to raise commodity prices to parity levels. The model was controversial from the outset—the Supreme Court struck down the processing tax that funded the program in *United States v. Butler* (1936)—but Congress swiftly reconstituted it through the Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act and a second Agricultural Adjustment Act, embedding the principle that the federal government bears a share of the risk inherent in farming.

The postwar decades brought successive reorganizations rather than retreat. The Agricultural Act of 1949 established the permanent price-support and loan framework that, technically, remains the statutory backstop for several commodities today. The 1950s and 1960s saw the introduction of the Soil Bank and, later, the payment-in-kind programs of the 1980s, which compensated farmers with surplus commodities rather than cash. The 1973 Farm Bill inaugurated target prices and deficiency payments, decoupling—at least partially—farm income support from commodity prices. The 1985 and 1990 farm bills added conservation compliance and export enhancement components, reflecting a broadening of subsidy rationales beyond price stabilization to include environmental stewardship and trade promotion.

The most consequential rupture came in 1996. The Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform Act—the "Freedom to Farm" Act—eliminated the New Deal-era deficiency payment system and replaced it with fixed, declining "production flexibility contracts," explicitly severing the link between subsidies and current prices or planted acreage. Proponents argued the transition would wean agriculture from federal support. The experiment lasted four years: collapsing commodity prices in 1998 and 1999 prompted Congress to pass a series of emergency supplemental packages, and the 2002 Farm Security and Rural Investment Act restored countercyclical payments and created the modern structure of direct payments, marketing loans, and price-linked support.

The 2014 and 2018 farm bills further reshaped the landscape, eliminating direct payments in favor of shallow-loss revenue programs—Agriculture Risk Coverage and Price Loss Coverage—and substantially expanding federally subsidized crop insurance, which has become the single largest federal farm support expenditure. The 2018 bill also legalized industrial hemp and expanded several conservation programs, illustrating the omnibus character of modern farm legislation.

This trajectory—from supply management to decoupled payments to revenue insurance—reflects a durable political coalition rather than a coherent economic theory. Urban and rural interests have long traded food assistance funding for farm program funding within a single legislative package, while commodity groups have defended and adapted the subsidy apparatus through every reform cycle. Understanding this history is essential to evaluating the contemporary debate, in which critics across the ideological spectrum question whether a Depression-era policy architecture, repeatedly retrofitted, remains suited to the structure of twenty-first-century agriculture.

text:
Thomas Brassey was born on 7 November 1805 in Buerton, Cheshire, the son of a farmer. His early education was modest, and at sixteen he was apprenticed to a land surveyor in Chester, work that introduced him to the practical mathematics of earthworks and gradients. In 1826 he entered the employ of the celebrated road builder Thomas Telford, and under Telford he learned the disciplines of estimating, contracting, and managing large bodies of labourers. When the railway age began, Brassey moved naturally into it. His first railway contract, for a section of the Grand Junction Railway near Penkridge, was undertaken in 1835 in partnership with William Mackenzie, a Liverpool contractor. The work was completed on time and to profit, and further contracts followed rapidly.

Brassey's distinctive contribution to nineteenth-century engineering was not invention but organisation. He perfected the system of the great public works contractor: he tendered for entire lines, assembled armies of navvies, and managed supply chains of brick, timber, and rails on an unprecedented scale. At his peak he employed some eighty thousand men across Britain, Europe, and beyond. He insisted on paying fair wages and providing decent conditions, and he was noted for the loyalty he inspired. His estimating was famously accurate; he once remarked that he had never lost money on a contract he had personally priced.

His British works included portions of the London and North Western, the Great Northern, and the Caledonian railways, as well as docks at Birkenhead and the great retaining wall at Holyhead. Abroad, he built the Rouen and Le Havre railway in France, lines in Belgium, Holland, and Italy, and the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada. In the 1850s and 1860s he undertook railways in India, Argentina, and Australia, often in partnership with the engineer Robert Stephenson and the financier George Stephenson's associates. The Crimean War brought him a contract for the Balaklava railway, a short line built to supply the besieging army, which was completed in a matter of weeks.

Brassey's methods shaped the profession. He demonstrated that a contractor could operate at continental scale, and his partnerships with engineers such as Stephenson, Locke, and the younger Brunel established the division of labour between designer and builder that characterised Victorian civil engineering. He was also among the first to adopt the railway navvy as a managed workforce rather than a casual rabble, though the conditions of navvy life remained notoriously rough.

He died on 8 December 1870 at St Leonards-on-Sea, having suffered a decline in his later years, partly through the failure of some overseas ventures and the dishonesty of a trusted agent. At his death his estate was modest compared with the scale of his operations, and his reputation rested on the thousands of miles of line he had caused to be built. His son, also Thomas Brassey, became a Liberal politician and was created Earl Brassey. The elder Brassey is remembered as the archetypal railway contractor of the Victorian age: a man of enormous energy, practical judgment, and organisational genius, whose name was attached to railways on four continents.

Central Bank Holds Interest Rates Steady as Inflation Cools

WASHINGTON, Oct. 15 — The central bank left its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Wednesday, holding borrowing costs at their current level for a second consecutive meeting as evidence mounted that inflation is gradually easing toward the bank's target.

The decision, widely anticipated by financial markets, keeps the policy rate in a range of 4.25 percent to 4.50 percent. Policymakers voted 9 to 2 in favor of the pause, with two dissenters arguing for a quarter-point reduction to shore up a slowing labor market.

In a statement released after the two-day meeting, the bank's policy committee said inflation had "continued to moderate" in recent months, citing softer readings on goods prices and a slower pace of shelter cost increases. Consumer prices rose 2.6 percent in the year through September, down from 3.1 percent in June and well below the four-decade high reached two years ago.

"Progress on inflation has been encouraging, but we are not yet at a point where we can declare victory," the bank's chair said at a news conference. "We want to see sustained evidence that inflation is moving durably toward 2 percent before considering any adjustment to the stance of policy."

The chair also acknowledged signs of cooling in the labor market, noting that monthly job gains had averaged about 120,000 over the past three months, down from roughly 200,000 earlier in the year. The unemployment rate ticked up to 4.3 percent in September. Still, officials described the overall economy as "expanding at a moderate pace," with consumer spending holding up better than many analysts had expected.

Financial markets showed little reaction to the announcement, as investors had priced in a hold with near certainty. Treasury yields were little changed, and major stock indexes closed marginally higher. Futures markets currently imply roughly a 60 percent probability of a quarter-point rate cut at the bank's December meeting.

Economists offered mixed interpretations of the decision. Some said the pause reflects a cautious approach as policymakers balance the risk of easing too soon against the risk of keeping rates restrictive for too long. Others suggested the committee is deliberately buying time to assess how quickly previous rate increases are still working through the economy.

"The bank is in wait-and-see mode," said one senior economist at a major research firm. "The inflation data are moving in the right direction, but the committee wants more confidence before it starts unwinding restrictive policy. December is live, but it is not a done deal."

The decision comes amid heightened political scrutiny of the central bank's independence. Lawmakers from both parties have pressed officials on the pace of rate adjustments, with some arguing that high borrowing costs are weighing on small businesses and housing affordability. The chair declined to comment on political matters, reiterating that policy decisions are made solely on economic grounds.

The bank also released updated economic projections, which showed officials expect inflation to reach 2 percent by the middle of next year, slightly later than previously forecast. Growth projections for the current year were revised up modestly, while the projected path of the policy rate suggested two quarter-point cuts next year, unchanged from the prior estimate.

Analysts said the central bank's next move will depend heavily on upcoming data, including two more inflation reports and a pair of employment surveys before the December meeting. For now, the bank appears content to hold steady and let the data speak.

"The bar for a move in either direction is high," the chair said. "We are prepared to respond as conditions evolve."

The bank's next policy meeting is scheduled for Dec. 9-10.

title: press release|a university announces a new research centre for battery technology
text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact: Elena Marsh, Director of Media Relations
University of Northumbria
e.marsh@northumbria.ac.uk | +44 (0)191 555 0142

Northumbria University Launches £28 Million Battery Innovation Centre with Industry Partners

*Newcastle upon Tyne, 14 October 2025* — The University of Northumbria today announced the establishment of the Northumbria Centre for Advanced Battery Science (NCABS), a £28 million research facility dedicated to next-generation energy storage. The centre, which opens its doors to researchers in March 2026, will focus on solid-state electrolytes, rapid-charging lithium-ion chemistries, and the recycling of critical minerals.

Funding for NCABS comes from a £12 million capital grant awarded by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), £9 million from the university’s own reserves, and £7 million in combined contributions from three industrial partners: Newcastle-based cell manufacturer Voltra Energy, German materials supplier BASF, and Japanese automotive firm Denso. The centre will occupy a 4,200-square-metre purpose-built laboratory on the university’s Coach Lane campus, creating 64 new research posts over the next three years.

Professor Amara Okonkwo, a materials chemist who joined Northumbria in 2019 from the University of Cambridge, will serve as NCABS’s founding director. Her team’s work on ceramic-polymer composite electrolytes was published in *Nature Energy* earlier this year and forms the basis for one of the centre’s first flagship projects.

“The gap between a promising lab result and a battery that survives 1,000 charge cycles in a real vehicle is where most technologies fail,” Okonkwo said. “NCABS is built to close that gap. We have the gloveboxes, the dry rooms, and — critically — the industrial partners who will tell us honestly when a material isn’t good enough.”

The centre’s three research programmes are already staffed with 22 doctoral students and 11 postdoctoral researchers. The first, led by Dr. Callum Reyes, targets solid-state batteries for electric vehicles, with a goal of demonstrating a 400 Wh/kg pouch cell by December 2027. A second programme, headed by Dr. Priya Ramanathan, examines direct recycling methods for recovering lithium, nickel, and cobalt from end-of-life cells; Voltra Energy will trial the recovered materials at its Blyth pilot line. The third, still in its early stages, will study sodium-ion chemistries for grid-scale storage, supported by a separate £2.1 million grant from the Royal Academy of Engineering.

Vice-Chancellor Professor Ian Whitfield framed the launch as part of a broader regional strategy. “The North East already builds more electric vehicles per capita than any other UK region,” he said. “What it has lacked is a world-class battery research base to match. NCABS changes that equation, and it does so with partners who have skin in the game.”

An official opening ceremony is scheduled for 19 March 2026, with UKRI Chief Executive Professor Dame Ottoline Leyser expected to attend. The centre will accept applications for its first cohort of industry-funded PhD studentships from 1 November 2025.

About the University of Northumbria
Founded in 1969, the University of Northumbria enrols approximately 37,000 students across its Newcastle and London campuses. Its energy research portfolio currently attracts £41 million in active grant funding.

About NCABS
The Northumbria Centre for Advanced Battery Science is a £28 million research facility operated in partnership with Voltra Energy, BASF, and Denso. It employs 33 researchers and support staff at launch.

text:
Hundreds of families have been forced to leave their homes after severe flooding swept through a Welsh valley following a night of torrential rain. Emergency services were called to the Afon Valley area in the early hours of Saturday morning as water levels rose rapidly, submerging roads and overwhelming drainage systems.

Rescue teams using boats and specialist vehicles evacuated more than 300 people from their properties, including elderly residents and young children. Local authorities have opened three rest centres in nearby community halls, where displaced families are being provided with shelter, food and warm clothing.

The flooding followed what forecasters described as an exceptional period of rainfall, with more than a month's worth of rain falling in less than twelve hours across parts of mid and south Wales. The Met Office had issued an amber warning for the region, but the intensity of the downpour exceeded expectations, catching some residents by surprise.

David Morgan, 67, who has lived in the valley his entire life, said he had never seen the river rise so quickly. "It came through the door before we knew what was happening," he said. "We've had floods before, but nothing like this. The water was up to my waist by the time the rescue boat arrived."

Another resident, Sarah Jenkins, described being woken by neighbours banging on her door shortly after 3am. "We grabbed what we could and just left," she said. "The children were terrified. We don't know what we'll find when we're allowed back."

The leader of the local council, Councillor Rhys Davies, said the scale of the operation was unprecedented for the area. "Our priority is the safety and wellbeing of residents," he said. "We are working closely with the emergency services, the fire and rescue service and the voluntary sector to ensure everyone has somewhere safe to stay."

Natural Resources Wales said river levels had peaked by mid-morning and were beginning to recede, but warned that further rain was forecast for the coming days. A spokesperson urged people to avoid travelling near rivers and to heed road closure signs, several of which remain in place across the valley.

The Welsh Government said it was monitoring the situation closely and had activated support arrangements for affected communities. A spokesperson expressed sympathy for those forced to leave their homes and praised the efforts of emergency responders.

Engineers are assessing the condition of bridges and roads, with some routes expected to remain closed for several days. Power has been restored to most properties after outages affected several hundred homes overnight, though some isolated areas remain without electricity.

Flooding has become an increasingly frequent concern in Welsh valleys, with communities calling for greater investment in flood defences. Local campaigners argue that ageing infrastructure has struggled to cope with more intense rainfall patterns in recent years.

The council has advised residents not to return to their homes until properties have been inspected and declared safe. An assessment of the damage is expected to begin once the water has fully receded, and officials have indicated that financial support will be made available to those affected.

For now, families in the valley face an anxious wait, uncertain of what they will find when they are finally allowed home. As one resident put it: "We've pulled together before. We'll do it again. But it's going to be a long road back."

Television pictures showed supporters running across the playing surface, with some appearing to approach opposing players before being led away.

The governing body said its disciplinary panel had taken a serious view of the events, noting that the invasion had placed players, officials and stewards at risk. The club has also been warned about its future conduct and could face stricter sanctions, including the partial closure of its stadium, if similar incidents occur again.

The club expressed regret over the disturbance and said it was reviewing its safety procedures. A spokesperson said the vast majority of supporters had behaved responsibly but acknowledged that a minority had put others in danger. The club confirmed it would increase steward numbers at forthcoming home matches and would work with local police to identify those who entered the field. It added that any supporter found to have taken part could face indefinite bans.

Player safety has become an increasingly prominent issue in recent seasons, with several high-profile matches interrupted by supporters running onto the pitch. Coaches and players have repeatedly called for stronger measures, arguing that unexpected contact with crowds can leave athletes vulnerable, particularly in tense or emotionally charged fixtures. Supporters groups, meanwhile, have urged clubs not to punish the wider fanbase for the actions of a few.

The incident has prompted debate about the balance between atmosphere and security at football grounds. The league is expected to review the case at its next meeting.

Letter to Shareholders

Fiscal 2024 was the year Harrow & Field stopped being a well-kept secret and became a regional operator in earnest. When we closed the books on March 31, 2025, we had grown from 34 stores to 47, added two new distribution spokes, and crossed $1.1 billion in net sales for the first time in our 61-year history—up 18.4% from $929 million the prior year. Same-store sales rose 3.9%, and adjusted EBITDA reached $71.2 million, a margin of 6.5%.

The headline, of course, was the acquisition of the eight-store Bellwether Markets chain in the Shenandoah Valley, which closed on August 12, 2024. We had courted the Bellwether family on and off since 2019, and I want to thank Ruth Bellwether for trusting us with a business her father opened in Winchester in 1971. All eight locations remained open through the transition, and we retained 94% of the store-level staff. The Bellwether banner came down in January, but the local buying team stayed—which matters more than the sign.

Organic growth mattered too. We opened four new stores during the year: Roanoke (May 2024), Frederick (July 2024), and two Charlotte-area locations in Huntersville and Matthews (October and February, respectively). We also completed major remodels at six older stores, including our original location on Market Street in Charlottesville, which reopened in November with a larger produce department and the first in-store tortilleria in our footprint. Remodeled stores are averaging a 9.2% sales lift in their first quarter back open, ahead of our 6% projection.

None of this came cheaply. Capital expenditures totaled $118 million, and we finished the year with $210 million in debt against $340 million in available liquidity. Our new distribution center in Lexington, scheduled to come online in September 2025, will be the largest single capital project in company history at $64 million. It is also, we believe, the difference between growing well and growing badly. Freight costs per case rose 11% this year largely because our older facility simply ran out of room.

Two people deserve particular mention. Chief Operating Officer Dana Whitfield ran the Bellwether integration personally, spending three days a week on the ground in Winchester for four months. And after 29 years with Harrow & Field—the last nine as our CFO—Marcus Bellamy will retire in August. His successor, Priya Raghunathan, joins us from Food Lion and has already been working alongside Marcus since February.

We know expansion carries risk. Two of our four new stores are still below their targeted weekly sales volumes, and we expect integration costs to weigh on first-half margins in fiscal 2025. We are not chasing store count for its own sake. The plan for the coming year is deliberately quieter: no acquisitions, two new stores in the Raleigh market, and the Lexington facility brought online on time and on budget.

Thank you for your continued confidence. We will see you at the annual meeting on July 17 in Charlottesville.

Sincerely,

Eleanor M. Cabot
President and Chief Executive Officer
Harrow & Field Markets, Inc.

title: medical patient information leaflet|managing type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise
text:
Managing Type 2 Diabetes with Diet and Exercise

Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition in which the level of glucose (sugar) in the blood becomes too high. It develops when the body does not produce enough insulin, or when the insulin it produces does not work effectively — a state known as insulin resistance. While medication is often part of treatment, diet and physical activity remain the foundation of effective management. For many people, sustained changes to what they eat and how much they move can lower blood glucose substantially, reduce the need for medication, and diminish the risk of long-term complications affecting the heart, eyes, kidneys, nerves and feet. This section explains what those changes involve and how to make them safely.

Diet

There is no single "diabetic diet." The aim is a balanced pattern of eating that controls blood glucose, supports a healthy weight and reduces cardiovascular risk. Carbohydrates have the greatest effect on blood glucose, because they are broken down into glucose during digestion. This does not mean excluding them; instead, choose slower-releasing, high-fibre sources — wholegrain bread and cereals, oats, brown rice, pulses and vegetables — in preference to refined products such as white bread, sugary drinks and confectionery. Spreading carbohydrate evenly across the day helps avoid sharp peaks and troughs.

Eating regularly, at consistent times, assists in keeping glucose stable, particularly for those taking insulin or certain tablets. Include protein with meals to promote fullness, and aim for at least five portions of fruit and vegetables daily. Choose unsaturated fats — olive and rapeseed oil, nuts, oily fish — over saturated fats found in processed meats, pastries and hard cheese. Limit salt and alcohol, and avoid foods high in added sugar. If you are overweight, losing even 5 per cent of your body weight can improve glucose control meaningfully; gradual, sustainable loss is preferable to restrictive dieting. A registered dietitian can tailor advice to your circumstances, culture and preferences.

Exercise

Physical activity lowers blood glucose by increasing the muscles' uptake of glucose and improving insulin sensitivity. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity weekly — brisk walking, cycling or swimming — spread over several days, together with two sessions of resistance exercise, such as light weights or body-weight exercises, to build muscle. Breaking up long periods of sitting with short walks offers additional benefit. Start gradually if you have been inactive, and choose activities you are likely to sustain.

Safety and monitoring

Check your blood glucose as advised, particularly when beginning a new activity, and carry a fast-acting source of sugar in case of hypoglycaemia — symptoms include shakiness, sweating and confusion. Inspect your feet daily, as reduced sensation can allow minor injuries to go unnoticed. Inform your healthcare team before making substantial changes, as medication doses may need adjustment. Small, consistent steps, reviewed regularly with your GP or diabetes team, are more effective than sudden drastic measures.

title: legislative bill text|an act requiring disclosure of data breaches within 72 hours
text:
AN ACT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF DATA BREACHES WITHIN 72 HOURS

Be it enacted by the Legislature of the State:

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

This Act may be cited as the "Data Breach Disclosure Act."

SECTION 2. LEGISLATIVE FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.

(a) Findings. The Legislature finds that:
(1) Personal information collected and maintained by public and private entities is increasingly subject to unauthorized access and acquisition;
(2) Delays in notifying affected individuals of a data breach substantially increase the risk of identity theft, financial fraud, and other harms;
(3) Existing notification requirements permit extended delay periods that fail to adequately protect consumers;
(4) A uniform seventy-two-hour notification standard will promote accountability, encourage robust security practices, and enable affected individuals to take timely protective measures.

(b) Purpose. The purpose of this Act is to establish a clear and expeditious obligation for entities that own or license personal information to disclose data breaches to affected individuals, the Attorney General, and relevant regulatory authorities within seventy-two hours of discovery.

SECTION 3. DEFINITIONS.

As used in this Act:
(1) "Personal information" means an individual's first name or first initial and last name in combination with any one or more of the following data elements: social security number; driver's license number or state identification card number; account number, credit card number, or debit card number in combination with any required security code, access code, or password; medical information; biometric data; or a username or email address in combination with a password or security question permitting access to an online account.
(2) "Data breach" means the unauthorized acquisition, or reasonable belief of unauthorized acquisition, of personal information that compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of such information maintained by an entity.
(3) "Entity" means any sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, association, governmental body, or other legal entity that owns or licenses personal information.
(4) "Discovery" means the first day on which an entity has actual knowledge of a data breach, or would have had knowledge through the exercise of reasonable diligence.
(5) "Affected individual" means a resident of this State whose personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person as a result of a data breach.

SECTION 4. NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS.

(a) General Rule. An entity that discovers a data breach shall disclose the breach to each affected individual, the Attorney General, and the principal supervisory authority for the entity's industry, if any, without unreasonable delay and in no event later than seventy-two hours after discovery.

(b) Content of Notification. The notification shall include, to the extent known:
(1) a description of the data breach, including the date or estimated date of the breach and the date of discovery;
(2) the categories of personal information involved;
(3) the number of affected individuals;
(4) the measures taken or proposed to be taken to remediate the breach and protect affected individuals;
(5) contact information enabling affected individuals to obtain further information; and
(6) advice regarding steps affected individuals may take to protect themselves, including recommendations to place a security freeze or fraud alert.

(c) Method of Notification. Notification to affected individuals shall be provided by written notice, electronic notice where the entity regularly communicates with the individual electronically, or telephone notice, provided that written notice is sent within five business days thereafter.

(d) Delayed Notification. An entity may delay notification only where a law enforcement agency determines that notification would impede a criminal investigation. Any such delay shall be documented in writing and shall not exceed thirty days absent written extension by the law enforcement agency.

SECTION 5. ENFORCEMENT AND PENALTIES.

(a) The Attorney General may bring an action to enforce this Act, including for injunctive relief and civil penalties of not more than one thousand dollars per day for each day notification is delayed beyond the period prescribed in Section 4, up to a maximum of one hundred thousand dollars per breach.

(b) A violation of this Act constitutes an unfair or deceptive trade practice.

SECTION 6. SEVERABILITY.

If any provision of this Act is held invalid, the remainder of the Act shall not be affected.

SECTION 7. EFFECTIVE DATE.

This Act shall take effect one hundred eighty days after enactment.

title: encyclopedia article|a species of freshwater turtle and its conservation status
text:
European Pond Turtle (*Emys orbicularis*)

The European pond turtle is a medium-sized freshwater chelonian and the sole living member of the genus *Emys* in Europe. Adults typically measure 12–20 cm in carapace length, though females, which grow larger than males, may reach 23 cm. The species was described by Linnaeus in 1758 as *Testudo orbicularis*; its current binomial dates to a 1764 designation by French naturalist Pierre Joseph Bonnaterre. The carapace is dark olive to blackish-brown, often stippled with fine yellow dots, while the head and neck are marked with longitudinal yellow streaks. A distinctive feature is the movable plastral hinge in juveniles, which stiffens with age.

The turtle's range is vast but fragmented, stretching from the Iberian Peninsula and Morocco eastward across Europe to the Aral Sea basin, with isolated populations in Iran and the Caucasus. It inhabits slow-moving waters—ponds, oxbows, marshes, and irrigation canals—with muddy bottoms and abundant aquatic vegetation. Females nest from May to July, laying 3–16 eggs in sandy or loamy soil; incubation lasts 60–90 days, and in cooler parts of the range embryos may overwinter in the nest. Hatchlings exhibit temperature-dependent sex determination. Individuals can live for over 60 years in captivity, with wild longevity estimates of 40–50 years.

Conservation status varies sharply across the range. Globally, the IUCN Red List assessed the species as Near Threatened in 1996, but a 2023 reassessment elevated it to Endangered, citing a population decline suspected to exceed 30% over three generations. The species is listed on Appendix II of the Bern Convention and Annexes II and IV of the EU Habitats Directive, requiring member states to designate protected areas. In Germany, where perhaps 5,000–8,000 individuals remain, the turtle is classified as Critically Endangered; the Brandenburg population, once numbering in the thousands, has contracted to a handful of ponds. Poland lists it as Critically Endangered, with fewer than 2,000 adults estimated in the 2010s. By contrast, populations in southern France and parts of the Iberian Peninsula remain comparatively robust.

Principal threats include wetland drainage and canalisation, which have eliminated an estimated 60% of suitable habitat in Central Europe since 1950; road mortality during nesting migrations; nest predation by foxes, raccoons, and wild boar; and competition and hybridization with introduced turtles such as the red-eared slider (*Trachemys scripta elegans*). Climate change poses a subtler risk: warmer summers skew hatchling sex ratios toward females, and drier springs desiccate nests.

Recovery efforts have gained momentum since the 1990s. Head-starting programmes in Germany, Poland, and Austria raise hatchlings in captivity for two to three years before release, improving juvenile survival from an estimated 5% to over 60%. Habitat restoration—reprofiling pond banks, creating nesting embankments, and removing invasive turtles—has been undertaken at sites in Brandenburg, the Łęczna-Włodawa Lakeland, and the Camargue. A LIFE-funded project, "LIFE EMYS," ran from 2014 to 2020 across Germany and Poland, releasing over 3,000 head-started turtles and restoring 40 hectares of wetland. Reintroduction attempts in Switzerland and the Netherlands, begun in the 2000s, remain provisional pending long-term breeding confirmation.

title: product review|a mid-range noise-cancelling headphone after three months of use
text:
Three Months In: The [Brand] [Model] Headphones

Verdict: A mid-range contender that earns its keep, with caveats

We've spent three months with the [Brand] [Model], a $249 over-ear noise-cancelling headphone positioned squarely in the crowded middle of the market. That's enough time for the honeymoon glow to fade—and for the small annoyances to either become background noise or grow into deal-breakers. Here's what held up, and what didn't.

 Noise Cancellation: Capable, Not Class-Leading

The [Model]'s active noise cancellation handles the essentials well. On a twice-weekly commuter rail line and several long-haul flights, it reliably flattened the low-frequency drone of engines and HVAC systems—the kind of constant rumble that wears you down over a long trip. Voices and higher-frequency clatter came through more than we'd like, particularly in a busy open-plan office, where the headphones muted the ambient hum but not the colleague two desks over. Against class leaders like the Sony WH-1000XM5 or Bose QuietComfort Ultra, the [Model] trails by a noticeable margin in the midrange. For the price, though, it's a credible performance, and the transparency mode is genuinely useful, piping in conversation with only a faint digital sheen.

 Sound Quality: Warm and Forgiving

Sonically, the [Model] leans warm. There's a gentle lift in the lower mids that flatters acoustic instruments and vocals, and the treble is smoothed rather than sparkling—comfortable for long listening sessions, if a touch shy on detail. Bass is present and controlled, though it doesn't dig as deep as the spec sheet's 20Hz claim suggests. Across three months of daily use—podcasts on the walk to work, playlists at the desk, the occasional album with full attention—the tuning proved agreeable rather than revelatory. The companion app's EQ is basic but functional; a modest cut around 200Hz cleaned up the low-end bloom considerably. Codec support is limited to AAC and SBC, with no aptX or LDAC, which is a real omission at this price for Android users.

 Comfort and Build: Quietly Competent

The [Model] is light—around 250 grams—and the clamping force strikes a sensible balance: secure enough for a brisk walk, loose enough that a three-hour flight didn't leave our glasses frames digging in. The earcups use memory foam wrapped in a soft synthetic leather that has shown no creasing or flaking after three months of near-daily use. The headband padding is adequate, if not generous. The plastic-heavy construction doesn't feel premium, but nothing has loosened, rattled, or squeaked. The hinges fold flat for packing, and the included hard case is a welcome inclusion at this price.

 Battery and Connectivity: The Strong Suit

Battery life has been the [Model]'s quiet triumph. Rated at 40 hours with ANC on, we averaged roughly 35 hours per charge across mixed use—enough that charging became a fortnightly chore rather than a nightly one. A ten-minute top-up yielded several hours of playback. Multipoint pairing, connecting to a laptop and phone simultaneously, worked without fuss, and reconnection after sleep was consistently quick. We logged only two dropouts in three months, both resolved by toggling Bluetooth.

 The Annoyances

The touch controls remain the weakest link. Swipes registered reliably perhaps eight times in ten, and volume adjustment—a vertical swipe on the right cup—was fussy enough that we largely abandoned it for the phone. The mics are serviceable for calls in quiet rooms but struggle outdoors; two colleagues independently described us as "distant" on a windy day. And the app, while stable, is sparse: no auto-off timer, no wear detection, no firmware changelog worth reading.

 After Three Months
